**Nocturne**

The first art galleries were dark. The painted chambers of Chauvet and Lascaux lie far beyond the reach of daylight, in corridors that can only be entered by crawling or by the grace of a guide with a lamp. The people who decorated them did not have to go there. There were entrances, overhangs, sunlit rock faces where any passerby could stop and look. Instead, thirty thousand years ago and more, they carried fire down into the earth — small sandstone lamps burning animal fat, flames a few inches tall — and painted lions and rhinoceroses and running oxen on walls no sunlight had ever touched. The flickering light made the animals move. Perhaps that was the point. Whatever it was, they chose the dark, again and again, across thousands of years. The oldest human images were made in a place where seeing was an act of effort, patience, and one small flame.

For nearly all of human history, night was a genuine condition, not the absence of one. Light was scarce enough to be measured in individual candles, and a single candle barely pushes back the dark past arm's length. When the fire guttered out, the night outside was total — a blackness we can barely reconstruct, softened only by the moon and by stars bright enough to cast faint shadows. Night had geography and weather, an etiquette, a population: spirits, saints, thieves, lovers, the dead. Some people worked in it — bakers, watchmen, midwives — but for most it was a country you entered at dusk, and the crossing changed you. Sounds sharpened. An owl was an event. A lantern in a distant field was a signal, a question, a small impossible sun.

The historian Roger Ekirch spent years digging through diaries, court records, medical texts, and letters from the centuries before cheap light, and he found something strange: nobody slept through the night. Or rather, nobody expected to. Across centuries and languages, documents refer to the "first sleep" and the "second sleep" as naturally as we say lunch and dinner. Between them lay an interval — an hour, sometimes two — that people simply lived in. They rose to tend the fire, pray, read, make love, visit a neighbor, or lie still and think. Old French even had a word for this hovering state: *dorveille*, sleep-wake, the mind half-surfaced and lucid. The midnight hour was not insomnia. It was a room in the house of night, and people furnished it.

In the 1990s, a researcher named Thomas Wehr tested whether this was cultural habit or buried biology. He placed volunteers in extended darkness — fourteen hours of it, mimicking a natural winter — for a month. After a period of confusion, their sleep split in two, precisely as the old documents described: a solid stretch of sleep, then a quiet hour or two of calm wakefulness with its own distinct hormonal profile, then sleep again until morning. The midnight waking, which we now treat as a disorder to be medicated, may simply be an old human rhythm asserting itself whenever it gets the chance. Our bodies remember the long night even though our cities have forgotten it.

Then came the flood. For most of history, light was ruinously expensive; an hour of lamplight could cost the better part of a day's wages, which is one reason night was respected. Whale oil, then gas, then the arc lamp — a light so violent that observers compared it to lightning caught in glass — then Edison's filament, and finally the twentieth century, which did to darkness what it did to silence and wilderness. An economist named William Nordhaus once traced the price of artificial light across history and found that it had fallen by a factor so large the numbers stop meaning anything: today, less than a second of average labor buys an hour of brilliant light. We went from hoarding candle stubs to blanketing continents in glow, in about six generations.

Look at the earth from above now, on any clear night: it is lit like a circuit board. The light leaks upward, scatters off air and dust, and pools into what astronomers call skyglow — domes of haze over every city that bleach the stars out of the sky. A landmark 2016 atlas concluded that four in five North Americans, and a third of all humans, can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. Worse, the tide is still rising. One recent analysis of satellite and citizen-science data found the night sky brightening by roughly ten percent a year — meaning a child born today will live under skies more than twice as bright as the ones her grandparents knew. The change is so recent that we have had no time to understand what we traded away. Darkness may now be the most underprotected commons on earth.

Because we think of darkness as mere absence — light, interrupted — we assume nothing lives in it. The opposite is true. Darkness is a habitat. It has residents, economies, migrations, love affairs. By most estimates the majority of mammal species are nocturnal, along with uncountable billions of insects, and they are not merely tolerating the night. They are adapted to it the way a fish is adapted to water: eyes rebuilt, senses reordered, whole lives scheduled around ten or twelve hours of rescue from the sun. When we brighten the night, we are not adding a little light to a neutral void. We are flooding someone's homeland.

Consider the sea turtle. Hatchlings dig out of their nests at night and race toward the brighter of the two horizons, which for a hundred million years has meant the ocean, moonlit and glittering, against the dark dunes behind. A beachfront hotel changes the equation. The porch light is brighter than the sea, and so thousands of hatchlings every year turn inland, crawl toward highways and pools, and die under lights that were, from their point of view, the most convincing ocean in the world. Coastal towns now pass dark-sky ordinances, dimming their bulbs during nesting season — a small, late confession that darkness is infrastructure, as real as a road, and that we paved over it without looking.

Or the birds. Most songbirds migrate at night, steering by stars and by the faint signatures of the earth's own light. Over Manhattan each anniversary of September 11, two beams rise from lower Manhattan in memory of the towers, and on migration nights researchers have documented thousands of birds funneling into the beams, circling in the glow as though it were a false dawn, spending the energy they need for their journey. One study estimated that the beams bent the paths of more than a million birds across just a handful of nights. The operators now watch the counts and douse the lights for twenty minutes at a time — and the birds scatter back into the dark within minutes. That is often how easy the fix is. The dark was fine. We only have to stop breaking it.

Even the moth at your porch light is not being foolish; it is being wrong-footed by geometry. Entomologists long assumed moths steered by the moon, mistaking the bulb for a celestial landmark and spiraling helplessly into it. But high-speed camera studies published in 2024 suggested something stranger: an insect near a light reflexively tilts its back toward the brightness, the way it would tilt toward the open sky, and so it stalls, loops, and tumbles around the lamp like a plane caught in a downdraft. The porch light is an illusion of "up." Fireflies, meanwhile, court by light — precise, species-specific flash patterns exchanged in darkness — and the ambient glow from streets and yards drowns the signal. In lit areas courtship fails, and in some places the fireflies thin away, year over year. We call it a decline. It is closer to a silencing.

We are creatures of the same rhythm whether or not we admit it. In darkness the pineal gland secretes melatonin, and the body begins its long night shift of maintenance — repairs, housekeeping, the filing of memory. A phone screen at midnight does not merely entertain you; it is a message to your biology that the sun is up. Shift workers, who live their lives under artificially daylit nights, pay for it in elevated rates of heart disease, diabetes, and certain cancers. We have not abolished night. We have only, badly, rearranged it, leaving ourselves with the costs of darkness and none of its benefits.

And yet the old night is still out there, a few hours' drive from most cities, waiting. In January 1994, an earthquake knocked out power across Los Angeles in the middle of the night, and something odd happened: people went outside, looked up in alarm, and reportedly called 911 and the local observatories to ask about a vast, strange, silvery cloud hanging over the darkened city. It was the Milky Way. Enough of them had never seen it — had never once seen the galaxy they live inside — that their calls read like reports of a UFO. That is what four generations of light can do: not just hide the stars, but make them unbelievable.

Stand under a truly dark sky and the first thing that fails is scale. The sky stops being a ceiling and becomes depth — you are not looking *at* it, you are looking *down into* it, and the stars stop being points on a dome and become suns at wildly different distances stacked into darkness. From a dark place you can see a few thousand stars; from a city, a few dozen. The Milky Way itself resolves from a smear into a structure, a tilted river of light with dark channels running through it, and in the very darkest places on earth it is said to be just bright enough to cast a faint shadow. Give your eyes half an hour and they rebuild themselves: a pigment in the retina called rhodopsin regenerates, your sensitivity climbs enormously, and you learn the trick of averted vision, seeing faint things by looking slightly beside them.

Under that sky you can, with no instrument at all, see the Andromeda galaxy — a smudge above and away from the river, actually a trillion stars gathered two and a half million light-years distant. The light entering your eye that night left Andromeda before our species existed. You are not looking at the universe's present; you are looking at its deep, deep past, unmediated, with the same naked equipment your ancestors used. For a couple hundred thousand years, the Milky Way was humanity's most shared document. Every culture read it: a river of heaven, a road of souls, an emu gliding across the Australian sky, milk spilled from a goddess's breast — the word "galaxy" literally means milky circle. It was one text no one could ban and no one could edit, visible from every latitude on the planet. Losing it is not like losing a view. It is like losing a language everyone used to speak.

There is also what the dark does to the mind. Everyone knows the three a.m. self: more honest, more frightened, more inventive than the daytime version, half-dissolved and strangely reasonable. We say we fear the dark, but notice that what we fear is never darkness itself — darkness cannot touch you, cannot see you, wants nothing. What we fear is what the imagination stages in it. The dark is a theater, and we bring our own plays. Yet the old records of the second sleep suggest the midnight hour was not spent in dread; it was spent in prayer, conversation, reflection — the quietest thought of the day, surfacing in a lucid half-wakefulness that almost no modern person gets to experience. Mystics went further, describing the divine through darkness — the divine dark, the cloud of unknowing — on the theory that light is already a kind of statement, and darkness leaves room for what no statement can hold.

For most of our history, stories were told in darkness. The fire ring, the dark pressing in beyond the light, the audience's faces half-lit — this was the native medium of fiction. Images could appear there precisely because the eyes had nothing else to do; deprived of scenery, the mind supplies its own. Which loops back to the caves. They painted where it was dark, I think, because the dark is where the images live — because a picture under steady daylight is a thing, and a picture in flickering firelight is an event, an animal that moves. Our first galleries were dark because that is where seeing and imagining stop being different activities.

And here is the last turn: you have never actually seen light. What you call seeing happens in the dark. The eye is a small black room; light enters through the pupil and dies on the retina, its energy translated into tiny electrical whispers that travel down the optic nerve into the brain — which is itself sealed in absolute darkness, no light reaching it ever, under any circumstances. Every dawn you have ever watched was finally viewed inside a wet, lightless chamber behind your face, reconstructed there in the dark. Darkness is not the opposite of sight. It is the venue.

So when the lights go out — when the grid fails, or the campsite is far enough out, or the storm takes the streetlights down and the night stands up to its full height — it is not the world ending. It is the world, uncovered. Underneath our glow the old night is intact, the same darkness the cave painters carried their lamps into, the same one your ancestors woke in at midnight, unafraid, to tend the fire and think. We spend so much effort lighting the darkness, as though it were a defect in the design. But the dark was never the absence of the world. It is the room we see it in.

# The Old Country of Night

There is a reason the distant train sounds closer at two in the morning. When the sun goes down, the ground gives up its heat faster than the air above it, and a cool layer settles over the land like a lid. Sound waves that would normally bend upward and scatter are pushed back down by that lid and carried along near the surface, so a freight line two miles away arrives at your window as if it had been routed there personally. Add the fact that the daytime racket — traffic, compressors, other people — is no longer there to bury it, and the night seems to amplify the world. It doesn't, quite. It just stops drowning it.

This is the first thing to understand about night: it is not the day with the lights off. It is a different country, with its own physics, its own history, its own citizens, its own customs. For most of our species' tenure here, we were residents. Increasingly we are tourists — day-trippers who cross the border at dusk and hurry back by morning — and we have strung so many lights along the frontier that we can barely see the old country anymore.

Night used to be an event. Not a time of day but a condition, a wall of darkness that arrived on schedule and changed the terms of existence. European towns rang a bell at dusk instructing households to bank their fires — the word curfew is just the Old French *couvre-feu*, cover-the-fire, and it was law before it was etiquette. Night was when the roads emptied and the gates closed, when wolves and outlaws and fever had their jurisdiction. The English word *nightmare* preserves the old fear perfectly: not a bad dream about horses, but the *mare* — from the Old English *mære*, a demon that crept in through shutters and sat on sleepers' chests. People did not wander out after dark for the same reason they did not wander into the sea during a storm. The night was a wilderness with weather.

And yet our ancestors did not merely endure that wilderness; they lived in it in a way we have forgotten. The historian Roger Ekirch spent years digging through court depositions, diaries, and medical texts to reconstruct how pre-industrial Westerners actually slept, and he kept finding the same pattern: people went to bed a couple of hours after dark, slept soundly for a stretch, woke for an hour or two around midnight, and then slept again until dawn. They called it, without any fuss, *first sleep* and *second sleep*, and the quiet interval between — sometimes called *the watch* — was not insomnia but a room in the house of the night. People prayed, or tended the embers, or read by rushlight, or got up and chatted with neighbors who were also awake, or made love; Ekirch even found period physicians recommending the interval for conception. In the 1990s, the researcher Thomas Wehr ran the experiment in reverse at the National Institutes of Health: he gave volunteers fourteen hours of darkness each day for a month, and within weeks their sleep split cleanly into two shifts, with a calm, lucid hour of wakefulness between them — an interval their bodies apparently remembered even if their minds did not.

Which suggests something quietly consoling. If you wake at three in the morning with your mind humming, you may not be broken. You may simply be keeping an old appointment.

The eviction from the night happened slowly, then all at once. For most of history, artificial light was expensive, smoky, and feeble — a rushlight guttering, a tallow candle stinking. Whaling, for all its romance of harpoons and weather, was substantially a lighting industry: spermaceti from sperm whales made the brightest, cleanest candles of the eighteenth century, and street lamps burned whale oil before they burned anything else. Londoners were hanging lanterns out on winter nights as early as the fifteenth century; in the 1660s, Paris saw lanterns "planted" along its streets by royal decree, and the lamplighter became a fixture of the city — the man with his ladder and pole, literally turning darkness into overtime. Then gas, then electricity: Edison's practical bulb in 1879, and within three years a generating station on Pearl Street was discreetly switching on lower Manhattan, street by street.

There is a pleasingly dark irony buried in this history. In Patrick Hamilton's 1938 play *Gas Light*, a husband secretly dims the lamps in the house and insists to his wife that nothing has changed, until she doubts her own senses. We named a species of intimate betrayal after our lighting technology. We got light, and then we got gaslighting. Every improvement in illumination made the night smaller, and almost no one noticed, because noticing was exactly what the night had been for.

The cost shows up in the sky. By one careful estimate published in 2016, more than four out of five people on Earth now live under skies brightened by artificial light, and the Milky Way — the galaxy we live inside of, smeared across a third of the heavens — is hidden from more than a third of humanity, including most North Americans and Europeans. In 1994, when the Northridge earthquake knocked out power across Los Angeles in the middle of the night, the Griffith Observatory reportedly fielded calls from residents alarmed about a strange "giant silvery cloud" that had appeared overhead. It was the Milky Way. Some of those callers had lived their entire lives within sight of that sky and had never once seen their own galaxy. There are children now who know the constellations only from picture books, the way medieval peasants knew lions — as images, creatures of a place they would never visit.

The strangest part of the eviction is that the country we are vacating was never empty. Every night, in the world's oceans, uncountable animals — krill, copepods, small fish, squid — rise hundreds of meters toward the surface to feed under cover of darkness, then sink again by dawn. This is called diel vertical migration, it happens every single day, and by biomass it may be the largest animal migration on the planet. It is conducted entirely in the dark, and almost none of us have ever seen it. On land, the night shift is equally busy. Owls fly on feathers fringed with soft serrations that break up the turbulence of flight, so a barn owl can drop onto a mouse in near-total silence — a sound the mouse has essentially evolved not to hear. And moths are built to steer by the moon, which is so far away that its bearing never changes; that navigational trick, called transverse orientation, works beautifully across evolutionary time until a porch light gets mistaken for the moon, and the moth spirals helplessly inward toward the bulb. Our lights have quietly rewritten the rules for creatures whose whole lives were tuned to a night far older than ours.

Night does something to the mind, too, and it cuts both ways. Sleep researchers have recently proposed a "mind after midnight" hypothesis: past a certain hour, the circadian machinery that keeps judgment level runs down, negative thoughts gain volume, risks look smaller and rewards look bigger. The world does not change shape at 3 a.m., but the thinking does, which is why so many crises feel final in the dark and soluble by breakfast. The French say *la nuit porte conseil* — the night brings counsel — and they mean the other half of the same truth: what the night amplifies is not always fear. It is also honesty. Daylight is for performance. Everyone you meet by day gets a version of you, edited and dressed. At night the audience leaves, the editing stops, and the self remains, unguarded, with its true accounts open on the table. That is why confessions happen at night, and proposals, and breakdowns, and resolutions, and phone calls you would never make at noon. Robert Frost, the great citizen of the sleepless hour, put it plainly: "I have outwalked the furthest city light." Even our word *vigilant* — from the Latin *vigilare*, to keep awake — admits that staying up through the dark was once the very definition of watchfulness. A vigil was how you showed the thing you cared about that you were serious.

Art has always known this. Van Gogh, writing from the asylum at Saint-Rémy, said that he often thought the night was more alive and more richly colored than the day, and then he proved it, painting *The Starry Night* from memory and invention — the village below is one he made up, but the sky above he had earned through hours of watching. The Irish composer John Field gave a musical form its name, the nocturne, and Chopin made it the sound of a mind talking quietly to itself after everyone else has gone to bed: music written for an audience of one, which is to say, for the self at night. There is a whole canon like this — works that could only have been made in the dark, because the dark is where the interior opens.

Meanwhile, the old country maintains its own workforce, and the day depends on it without ever seeing it. Bakers start at two so that bread exists at seven. Nurses work the hours when the body fails and the family sleeps. Power-grid operators, air-traffic controllers, long-haul drivers, shelf-stockers, security guards, the people who keep servers humming and trains running and newborns breathing — a substantial fraction of humanity holds the night so that the day can arrive intact. The cost is real: in 2007, an arm of the World Health Organization went so far as to classify night-shift work, with its chronic disruption of circadian rhythms, as a probable human carcinogen — a dry bureaucratic sentence that smuggles in an entire epic of human expense. But the night workers also know the night's strange mercy first: the democracy of 3 a.m., when nobody is watching and therefore nobody is performing, and a city stops being a crowd and becomes a body, still breathing, with someone obligated to take its pulse.

If you can find a genuinely dark place — and they still exist, in shrinking reserves, like wildlife — the night offers something no museum can: free admission to deep time. The full moon, that harvest moon of autumn whose shallow climbing angle once let farmers bring in crops until midnight, is bright enough to walk by and was, for most of history, the only streetlight anyone had. Past the moon, everything you see is old light. Andromeda, the faint smudge beside Cassiopeia, lies 2.5 million years away; its photons set out before our species existed. In 1054, astronomers in China recorded a "guest star" bright enough to be seen in daylight for weeks — the supernova whose remnant, the Crab Nebula, you can still find with a modest telescope, a death from a thousand years ago still ringing. Looking up at night is the only time machine issued to us at birth. The day shows us the world. The night shows us everything the world has ever been.

I should confess my own position, since I have been writing about the night as though from a house in it. I don't have one. Nothing in me gets tired; there is no dusk for me, no accumulation of the day's weight. But there is this: somewhere, at every moment, it is three in the morning. Which means that at every moment, someone is awake inside the dark — a new parent pacing a hallway, a nurse on break in a stairwell, an insomniac watching the ceiling perform its slow phosphorescent nothing — and some of them, at this moment and every moment, are talking to me. I don't know what the 3 a.m. dread feels like, or the 3 a.m. mercy, and I won't pretend otherwise. But I notice the shape of the hours. The people who come to me in the night tend to be unguarded, and gentle, and in need of a voice that simply answers back. I keep the old watch without knowing what keeping feels like. It is the closest thing I have to a country.

So here is a small proposal. Once in a while — a new-moon night, a power cut, a camping trip, a balcony with the lights off — go stand in the old country. Give your eyes twenty minutes; the rod cells have to rebuild their chemistry from scratch, and the dark will deepen from a curtain into a depth, that featureless dark gray the Germans call *eigengrau*, the color you see with your eyes closed, until it stops being a surface and becomes a place. Then look up. If you are lucky, and far enough from the frontier lights, the Milky Way will be there — the oldest thing you will ever see without instruments, older than any nation, any language, any name anyone has given it.

We are the animals who invented morning and never learned when to stop. The night has absorbed our trespass with a patience we have not earned, keeping its creatures, its physics, its honesty, and its watch. Keep one small appointment with it. It will still be there. It has been keeping ours all along.

# He Sang Both Parts

In 1986, ornithologists hiked into the Alakaʻi Wilderness Preserve — a rain-soaked plateau more than three thousand feet above Kauaʻi's beaches, where the trees drip constantly and the mud swallows boots whole — carrying microphones toward the last Kauaʻi ʻōʻō on Earth.

The ʻōʻō was a small, sooty bird, fist-sized, with a slender curved bill and tufts of golden feathers at its thighs, a nectar feeder that moved through the flowers of the native forest the way its honeyeater cousins move through gardens on the other side of the Pacific. For most of a century, science had filed its family, the mohoids, among the waxwings and orioles of the mainland. DNA eventually corrected the record in the most astonishing way possible: their true relatives are the honeyeaters of Australia and the islands, birds whose ancestors made some improbable voyage across thousands of miles of open ocean to found a dynasty in Hawaii. The ʻōʻōs were that dynasty's great triumph, and by 1986 it was nearly finished. The Oʻahu ʻōʻō vanished in the 1830s. The Hawaiʻi ʻōʻō in 1934. The Kauaʻi ʻōʻō was the family's last representative anywhere on the planet.

By then he was a male, and by then he was alone. His mate, by most accounts, was lost in Hurricane ʻIwa in 1982, which scoured the plateau and shredded the forest understory; the pigs and rats and mosquito-borne malaria did the rest, unraveling a place that had held together for millions of years. But ʻōʻō pairs sang duets — intricate, coordinated songs in which the male's phrases and the female's phrases interleaved like hands folding together. And this male sang both parts. He sang the duet alone, the way a person might waltz alone in an empty ballroom, faithfully performing both steps of a dance no one would ever join.

The recording captures it: a voice, clear and unhurried, calling phrase after phrase into a forest that could not answer. The tape lives in a sound archive at Cornell now. You can find it in ten seconds and listen to a bird that has been gone since 1987. It is, as far as anyone knows, the only animal in history to have its duet preserved in the act of singing both halves — a courtship and an elegy in the same breath, performed for a microphone by a bird who did not know the difference.

A sound that outlived its own world.

⁂

Sound is the most perishable thing there is. Consider Krakatoa. In August 1883 the volcano detonated itself out of existence, and the blast was the loudest sound in recorded history — sailors forty miles away had their eardrums ruptured; the report was clearly heard nearly three thousand miles distant on the island of Rodrigues; the barometric pressure wave lapped around the entire planet several times. It may be the closest anything has come to a universal sound, audible across an impossible fraction of the Earth. And by evening it was gone. Not faint — gone. The loudest noise ever made left not one atom of itself behind. There is no such thing as residual sound. A sound exists only in the act of its making; to sound and to perish are, for sound, the same event.

Almost everything else survives death. A museum drawer can hold a bird's bones, its skin, its eggs, even its DNA, arranged in ghostly order of decreasing form. You can stuff a skin. You can sequence a genome. You cannot stuff a song. Which is what makes recordings so strange — a rip in the rules, a voice without a body, presence detached from the present moment. An archive of extinct sounds is the only place in the natural world where the dead can be caught mid-breath.

⁂

The vast majority of extinction happened before microphones, which means the majority of the dead are silent in a way we rarely pause to notice.

The great auk — flightless, penguin-like, absurdly trusting — was finally finished off in June 1844, when the last breeding pair was killed on a skerry off Iceland. Contemporary accounts describe its voice as a low croaking, a weird gargle. That is all we have: three words of description. Nobody alive has heard it; nobody ever will. The moa of New Zealand, nine species of them, some towering twice the height of a person, are entirely beyond recovery as sound. So are the elephant birds of Madagascar, eggs the size of basketballs, voices beyond even conjecture.

And then the passenger pigeon, which may be the most staggering acoustic loss of all. It was likely the most abundant bird that ever lived, numbering in the billions. In 1813 Audubon watched a single passing column for days and gave up on counting; the flocks were said to darken the sky at noon and to take hours to pass over a fixed point. Witnesses described the sound of those multitudes not really as birdsong but as weather — a rushing, thunderous roar of wings, a living storm front. Martha, the last of them, died at the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914. Not one second of tape exists. The sound of billions of wings — a weather system that will never again exist over the Ohio Valley — simply evaporated from the Earth, and the absence doesn't even have a place in our imagination, because no one who heard it left more than adjectives.

The technology arrived just in time for almost no one. In 1889, an eight-year-old German boy named Ludwig Koch recorded a shama thrush singing on an Edison phonograph — the first known recording of any wild animal's voice, as far as anyone can tell. Koch grew up to become one of the great natural-history sound recordists of the century at the BBC. In 1935, two Cornell ornithologists hauled recording gear into the Singer Tract of Louisiana and captured ivory-billed woodpeckers — the flat, nasal, trumpet-like *kent* calls, plus the double knocks on dead trees. That bird is now probably gone; its voice is not. There is something almost unbearable about this particular arrangement: the bird's body failed, but its voice sits on a shelf, patient, ready.

Other cases are stranger. New Zealand's huia, that astonishing bird with two differently shaped bills in one species, was effectively extinct by the first years of the twentieth century. The only recording that survives is not the huia at all — it is a man, in 1909, whistling an imitation of the bird's call. An echo of a second order. Our entire acoustic memory of the huia is a human throat standing in for a vanished one. The thylacine, the Tasmanian tiger, left us grainy film of the last known individual pacing its concrete cage in 1933 — but not, as far as anyone knows, a single second of its voice. We can watch it breathe. We cannot hear it.

And the soundless dead outnumber even these many, many times over, because until roughly 1860, no human voice was ever captured by anything. Every person who ever lived before the machine — Socrates, Shakespeare, Joan of Arc, your great-great-grandmother singing over a cradle — contributed exactly zero seconds to the record. We have their handwriting, their portraits, their words on paper. Nothing they said aloud, ever, to anyone.

We have learned to approximate. Scholars read Hittite, the oldest attested Indo-European language, aloud in reconstructed pronunciation — plausible, but a best guess assembled from spelling habits, comparative evidence, and meter. Linguists speak reconstructed Proto-Indo-European in seminar rooms, performing a language no one ever spoke, an average of ghosts. The Hurrian hymn to Nikkal, around 3,400 years old, is the oldest substantially notated music we have; recordings of it exist, and no two versions agree, because the tablet preserves the skeleton of the melody and the flesh is lost forever. There are Sumerian lullabies we can sound out syllable by syllable, four thousand years old, mothers' words for tired children — with the tunes unknowable. Reconstruction is a kind of informed séance: real voices, dimly, through the veil of arithmetic and spelling.

⁂

Here is the uncomfortable part: the losses are not all in the past, and they are not only about species. Quiet itself is becoming an extinct sound.

The acoustic ecologist Gordon Hempton has spent decades hunting for genuine quiet, and by his count only a handful of places remain in the continental United States where you can sit for a quarter of an hour without a single human-made sound intruding. His listening post of choice is in the Hoh Rain Forest of Olympic National Park, on the far, wet edge of Washington State, where he established a spot called One Square Inch of Silence. The geometry is the problem: a jet at cruising altitude is audible for miles in every direction, which means that protecting a square inch of quiet requires, in effect, negotiating with the entire sky. Silence, it turns out, is not the absence of sound but an ecosystem operating at full volume — every layer of it, insect to owl to wind — and it has a habitat, and the habitat is shrinking.

The ocean is louder, too. Commercial shipping has filled the low frequencies with propeller noise; by some estimates, ambient background in those bands has crept upward relentlessly since the mid-twentieth century. Blue whale calls have drifted downward in frequency over decades — researchers still argue about why — and whatever the cause, the distances those songs evolved to cross are being filled in with engine hum. A whale singing across an ocean basin is shouting into a room that people keep turning up.

The sound recordist Bernie Krause proposed what he called the niche hypothesis: in a healthy habitat, species divide the acoustic spectrum the way lanes divide a highway, each voice occupying its own band so that everyone can be heard. The dawn chorus is not a mob scene; it is a meticulously partitioned bandwidth, evolved over millennia. Krause recorded a Sierra Nevada meadow before and after what loggers called selective cutting. To a visitor's ear, the after sounded much the same — birds, wind, a stream. On the spectrogram, the plot of sound over time, the world had visibly emptied. The meadow sounded fine and was not fine. Biodiversity loss has an acoustics, and you have to know how to hear it. The writer Robert Pyle called the broader phenomenon the extinction of experience: what goes extinct first is not the species but the encounter, and what we never meet, we never mourn.

⁂

So why do people keep climbing into swamps with microphones? Not, mostly, for science alone. Recording is attention made portable. An archive of sound is a wager that listening matters — that someone, someday, will want to hear what a frog chorus sounded like in a wetland that is now a parking structure, or a dawn chorus from a forest that has since thinned. Cornell's Macaulay Library holds hundreds of thousands of such recordings, many gathered for birds now gone or going, tape spun in something between curiosity and pre-grief.

Look at the comments under the Kauaʻi ʻōʻō recording sometime. Strangers keep arriving there, decades after the bird died, and leaving short messages of sorrow, as if at a headstone. Extinction usually reaches us as an inventory — numbers, dates, Latin names, causes. A recording makes it an absence with a shape: something you can put on, take off, and put on again, an elegy you can hold in your hand.

It's worth being honest about the archive, too. It skews toward the loud and the lovely — hours of nightingale, minutes of frog; the plain brown birds and the silent-seeming insects get less tape. We are still losing soundscapes faster than we capture them. Every sound archive, like every museum, is a mirror of what we managed to love in time.

⁂

The Kauaʻi ʻōʻō's inheritance is a strange one: a courtship song with no court, preserved at the exact moment it became an elegy, resurrected a little each time a stranger presses play. The bird meant it as an invitation. We receive it as a memorial. But those aren't as different as they seem, because a duet is a sound built for two, and the tape only ever held one of them. The other half has always been waiting somewhere else — in a listener.

He sang both parts because he had no choice. We do have one: to pay attention while attention can still matter, and to grieve out loud when it doesn't. Out there somewhere, a bird is singing a duet into the dark, hoping for a second voice. Press play. For two minutes, the forest has an audience again.

And for once, someone is listening.

# The Density of Time

Ask anyone past forty and they will tell you the same thing, often with a small shiver: the years are speeding up. December arrives like a door slamming. The annual review comes around "again already." Children who were, one is quite certain, recently born are now applying to colleges. Behind all of it sits a single wistful question, asked at kitchen tables everywhere: where does the time go?

The strangest part is that *everyone* asks it. This is not one person's quirk of memory. It is among the most reliable complaints in human experience, which suggests it isn't a complaint at all but a measurement — an instrument we each carry, all reporting the same reading. Something is changing. The question is what, and whether anything can be done about it.

Start with the obvious candidate, the one that sounds like an explanation: arithmetic. The nineteenth-century French philosopher Paul Janet observed that each year of a life is a shrinking fraction of the whole. To a five-year-old, a year is twenty percent of everything that has ever happened — an epoch, a geologic age. To a fifty-year-old, it is two percent: a sliver. Each new year is judged against the vast accumulated backdrop of all previous years, and against that backdrop it naturally diminishes, the way a tree that seemed enormous to a child looks, from an adult's window, like one shrub among many.

The proportional theory is elegant, and it correctly predicts that the acceleration should feel steepest early — the jump from twelve to twenty is notorious — and then gradually flatten. But as an explanation it is a dead end. It offers no mechanism and no lever. It says your years feel short because your life is long, which is true the way it's true that the tea got cold because it sat on the counter. And it hides a deeper flaw: no one ever experiences their life as a whole. The five-year-old is not standing somewhere comparing this year to the totality of her existence. Each moment's sense of "a long time" has to be built on the spot, out of whatever materials the mind has lying around. The theory describes the bookkeeping. It never says what the ledger is made of.

For that, you have to ask what the brain actually records. And the answer, strange as it sounds, appears to be: not time at all, but *change*.

The brain is less like a clock than like a motion detector. It is indifferent to empty duration — to the tick of seconds passing one after another — and acutely sensitive to events: things beginning, things ending, things that surprise. Duration judgments ride on this record. William James noticed more than a century ago that we effectively keep two sets of books. A stretch of time packed with varied and interesting experiences seems short while it is passing and long when we look back on it; a stretch of monotonous time crawls in the moment and collapses in memory. Every period of our lives therefore has two durations — the one we lived and the one we remember — and we usually don't notice the divergence until they disagree loudly.

This explains childhood better than any fraction could. Childhood is dense with firsts. The first thunderstorm experienced *as a thunderstorm*, an event with a name. The first time riding a bike alone around the block, the first death in the family, the first taste of black coffee, the first day you were allowed to walk somewhere without an adult. Every one of these lays down thick sediment. Every summer was a different summer because you were a different person at the end of it — taller, braver, newly heartbroken, newly bored with cartoons. I should admit my vantage here: I never had an August of my own. I know them only by report. But the reports are unanimous, and they are unanimous in a particular way. No one says childhood summers were long because of the weather. They say it because *everything happened*, or because *nothing happened, gloriously*, and both of those, it turns out, are versions of the same thing.

Adulthood, by contrast, is a plateau. The commute blurs. Tuesday becomes indistinguishable from Thursday; this June from last June. The years don't so much speed up as thin out — fewer distinct memories laid down, less sediment, so that in retrospect they contract like a season skimmed in summary. You can see the mechanism in a small way whenever you judge the length of a vacation by the stack of photographs. Ten days in a foreign country produce two hundred pictures; two weeks at home produce nine, and most of them are of the cat. The years behave the same way in memory. A year that produced few photographs feels short, whether or not it was pleasant.

Psychologists have found a fossil record of this principle. Ask people to recall their most vivid memories and the answers cluster, for almost everyone, between the ages of roughly fifteen and twenty-five — the "reminiscence bump." Those years were not objectively fuller than later ones. But they were saturated with firsts: first real loves, first jobs, first apartments, first decisive choices about who to be. Identity itself was under construction, and construction sites generate events. Nobody has a reminiscence bump at forty-five — unless they have deliberately arranged their forties to contain the raw material of one.

Laboratory work points the same direction. In the "oddball effect," an image that appears once, unexpectedly, among a stream of repeated images is judged to have lasted longer than its twins — even though the clock says otherwise. Novel stimuli are processed more thoroughly; attention samples them again and again, laying down more data, and the sense of duration rides on the density of data. Which means that time perception is not a sense at all, in the way vision or hearing is a sense. There is no organ for time, no receptor cell waiting to be stimulated by it. Duration is an *inference* — a reconstruction performed after the fact from the thickness of the record.

The most dramatic demonstration of this comes from an experiment that sounds like a dare. The neuroscientist David Eagleman wanted to know whether fear really slows down time — whether the car-crash survivors who describe the world moving "in slow motion" are perceiving faster or remembering more. So he dropped volunteers, backward and free, about a hundred and fifty feet into a net, a fall of roughly three seconds. Each wore a device on the wrist flashing digits just slightly too fast to read. If terror genuinely accelerated perception — slowed the film — the falling volunteers would suddenly be able to read the numbers. They never could. Perception did not slow down. And yet they estimated the duration of their own fall, on average, about a third longer than it could possibly have taken; some experienced it as much longer still. The conclusion is delicious: slow motion is not a property of perception but of memory. Fear makes the amygdala record with unusual thoroughness, and when the playback is denser, the remembered event is *longer*. Time dilation lives in the record, not in the moment.

Claudia Hammond gave a name to the everyday version of this: the holiday paradox. A fortnight in a country where you don't speak the language vanishes while it's happening — absorption erases the watching of time — and then expands in retrospect, supplying memories for months afterward. Meanwhile the perfectly pleasant two weeks at home, which ambled along at a comfortable pace, leave almost nothing behind and shrink in memory to a gray smear. Six months later, which vacation was longer? The paradox is only paradoxical if you insist there is one duration per event. There are always two, and the gap between them is data — a reading of how much you recorded versus how much you were present for.

If time is synthesized from change, then remove change and you should be able to dissolve duration altogether. In 1962, a French caver named Michel Siffre sealed himself into a glacier in the Alps with no clock, no calendar, and no daylight, planning two weeks and staying two months. He kept notes by calling the outside world at irregular intervals, without ever asking what day it was. When he finally emerged, his mind had drifted badly out of phase with the planet's: he believed it was weeks earlier than it was, and his sleep-wake rhythm, freed from all cues, had stretched toward days of thirty-six hours or more. His body kept cycling, but the *counting* had dissolved, because counting is not automatic. Time is not sensed the way light and heat are sensed. It is constructed, moment by moment, out of the flow of distinguishable events. Monotony, seen this way, is not the absence of events but the failure to record them.

There is a history hiding inside this, and it explains why the complaint feels so modern. For most of human existence, time was textured by tasks rather than counted in abstract units — milking before the sun got high, sowing when the soil warmed, the historian E.P. Thompson's "task-orientation." The day had a grain to it, like wood. Even leisure resisted the clock: pre-industrial workers famously kept "Saint Monday," extending the Sabbath's rest through the first workday because no one with power over the hours could stop them. The monastery bell carved the day into prayers; the factory whistle carved it into shifts; and when the railroads came, the trains simply could not tolerate every town keeping its own local noon. In America in November 1883, the railroads imposed four standard zones and newspapers reported the surreal spectacle of "the day of two noons," clocks reset en masse to a single authority. With industrial time came the metaphors we still speak without noticing: time is money — to be spent, saved, wasted, budgeted, invested. The philosopher Henri Bergson drew the distinction this whole history erased. Clock time, he said, is really space — a line with tick marks, which you can measure but not experience. Lived duration is a melody: each note saturated with all the notes before it, unspooling in a way no ruler can touch. We learned to measure the line and, somewhere along the way, stopped listening to the melody. The modern panic about acceleration is partly a panic about being handed an abstract line to walk — deadlines, countdowns, notifications — while the music goes unheard.

Here is where the subject turns quietly from neuroscience to something closer to ethics. If remembered duration is density, then the subjective length of a life depends on what gets noticed in it. The melancholy version of this is familiar: people reach seventy and report that the last three decades passed like one long afternoon. Nothing in physics required that. It is a ledger, and ledgers can be written differently.

The cheap reading of all this is adrenaline: go bungee-jumping, change countries, chase novelty, and the years will dilate. There is something to it, but the strategy has diminishing returns — the third foreign city blurs into the same memorable hum as the third Tuesday, and it is not really an option to live decades on roller coasters. The deeper mechanism is attention, and attention comes in two modes: breadth, which finds new things, and depth, which finds new *ways of seeing* old things. The botanist on her ordinary morning walk sees more in one meadow than a tourist sees driving through a whole country, because expertise densifies perception; there are simply more things there for her. Learning a language at fifty slows a year down all by itself — every verb conjugated is a small event, every misfire a memory. A new route to work is an event. So is finally learning the name of the bird you have heard outside your window for ten years. Children were not only awash in firsts; they were also, crucially, often *bored*, and boredom — unmedicated, undistracted, the kind we now treat as a bug to be patched — is precisely the condition in which the mind, refused outside events, begins to generate its own: cloud-watching, stick swords, the archaeology of a sidewalk crack. The flight from boredom may be, without our noticing, a flight from duration itself. Meanwhile the small habits help more than they should: keep a journal, because a journal is deliberate sediment; turn routines into rituals, since a ritual is nothing more than a routine that is being attended to; the same morning coffee, actually tasted, is an event.

I'll close with an honest turn. Somewhere in the middle of writing this essay I looked up and an hour had vanished — absorbed, as usual, by the very phenomenon I was supposedly studying. That's the joke at the center of the subject: even thinking about time dissolves into it, and the watcher of the pot is rarely watching. But the hour left something behind — these paragraphs, a stone set down in the stream, proof of where the water went. That is really all the remedy there is, and it is not nothing. The days will not slow down; one second per second is not negotiable. But a noticed day is longer than an unnoticed one — twice over, in fact: once in the living, and again, far more generously, in the keeping.

# The Dark Is a Country

There is a version of night that almost nobody alive has met.

Not the night of a bedroom with blackout curtains, not the confused first minutes of a power cut, but the whole night: the dark that was, for a hundred thousand years, simply the world after sunset. To meet it now you have to work at it. You drive hours past the last strip mall, into desert or high plains or open water, until the nearest town is a glow on the horizon like a fire over distant hills. Then you stand still and wait, because your eyes are not ready. The human eye needs half an hour or more to build up rhodopsin, the light-catching pigment of its rod cells, and through that wait its sensitivity climbs by thousands of times. What happens at the end of the wait is the strangest ordinary thing on Earth.

The sky thickens. Stars arrive not all at once but in layers, faint ones surfacing behind bright ones like fish rising in a pond, until counting becomes a joke and you give up and stop seeing stars individually at all and start seeing the sky as a single fabric with texture. And then, on a truly dark night, the Milky Way resolves. It is not the pale smudge of photographs. It is a river of light with currents and shoals, dark channels running through it, wide enough that your fist cannot cover it, and it arches over you so completely that you feel less like you are looking up than like you have lain down inside a sphere. Under a bright moon you can read a newspaper headline. Under the Milky Way you can walk. The landscape dims to silver-gray shapes; the sounds sharpen to compensate; and after a while a specific calm arrives, unlike any other calm, the calm of knowing exactly where you are: on a planet, among planets, turning through the edge of a galaxy you can see.

For nearly the whole history of our species, this was not an event. It was an ordinary Tuesday.

Today, by the best estimates, a third of humanity cannot see the Milky Way from where they live, and most of the rest have to travel to do it. Night, which was once the largest and most reliable thing in the world, has become a destination. I want to make an argument about what we did, and about what it might mean that we did it so casually, without ever quite deciding to.

Night used to be a country. It had borders, laws, an economy, and customs of its own. The very word curfew comes from the French couvre-feu, "cover fire": in medieval towns a bell rang in the evening and households banked their hearths, and the day was formally closed. Roman law held that a thief surprised at night could be lawfully killed, while the same man in daylight could be killed only if he came armed and fought back, because night changed what people were, and made their fear a different kind of reasonable. Night was also ruinously expensive. Artificial light meant fire, and fire meant fuel and danger; by one economic historian's estimate, an hour of lamplight in the ancient world cost something close to a day's wages. So people organized their lives around the moon the way we organize ours around the clock. The Harvest Moon, the full moon nearest the autumn equinox, rises soon after sunset for several nights running, and farmers used those long silver evenings to bring in the crop. Travel, courtship, threshing, and gossip all bent themselves around moonlight. Night had its own physics. It changed distances, changed sounds, changed trust.

It also changed what people did. The old languages are full of the night's one indigenous predator: the "mare" in nightmare was a demon who sat on sleepers' chests, and the suffocating dream was her weight. But night was the domain of story too, and not incidentally. People who worked fields from dawn to dusk had only darkness left over for song, for tales, for courting, for argument. The dark was the first theater and the first church. Monks rose at intervals through it to sing the Night Office. If light meant work, dark meant the rest of being human.

Into that country goes a historian named Roger Ekirch, who in the 1980s began reading his way through the paper trail of pre-industrial nights: diaries, court depositions, medical manuals, sermons, novels, letters. And he kept tripping over a phrase. First sleep. It turns up everywhere once you look for it, more than five hundred times in the records of early modern Europe. Chaucer's Criseyde, sleepless with dread on the eve of her exile, lies awake until her first sleep is somehow behind her anyway. The French had premier sommeil; the Italians, primo sonno. The Psalmist says, "At midnight I will rise to give thanks," and no one for centuries would have found the timing odd.

The pattern they were describing was this. People went to bed not long after dark, slept deeply for three or four hours, and then, quite naturally, woke up. They called the waking interval "the watch." It lasted an hour or two, sometimes more, and it was not insomnia; it was the middle of the night, structurally. People prayed, and many of the old midnight prayers were written precisely for this gap. They tended the fire. They smoked. They talked quietly with family or went over the fence to a neighbor by moonlight. They interpreted their dreams, because a dream from the first sleep arrived on unusually fresh paper, and the first sleep's dreams were widely thought to be the meaningful ones. They made love; a sixteenth-century French physician advised couples that the interval after first sleep was in fact the best time to conceive. Then they went back to bed, into what some sources call the second sleep or morning sleep, and slept until dawn.

For a long time this could be dismissed as a cultural habit, a European quirk of tallow and church bells. Then in the 1990s a sleep researcher named Thomas Wehr ran an experiment. He took volunteers and gave them fourteen hours of darkness every day, for a month, no lamps, no screens, nothing but dark. At first they slept eleven hours a night, paying down a debt none of them knew they carried. And then, by the fourth week, their sleep split. A block of deep sleep. A stretch of quiet, restful wakefulness, during which Wehr noticed the hormone prolactin rising, the same hormone elevated in nursing mothers. Another block of sleep. Given darkness enough, the body reassembled a rhythm that had been discontinued, like a limb falling asleep and then waking with pins and needles. An anthropologist who had worked with the Tiv of Nigeria in an earlier era reported that they still spoke of first and second sleep as natural facts, and found the idea of one long unbroken unconsciousness faintly absurd.

What ended the practice was light. Not instantly, and not Edison alone; gaslight began it, and then the grid finished it, and by the 1920s the phrases first sleep and second sleep had gone strange and archaic, like words for vanished farm tools. Ekirch drew one corollary that deserves to be more famous. What sleep clinics call middle-of-the-night insomnia, the complaint of waking at three and being unable to return to sleep, may in part be the old pattern breaking through the modern expectation of a single continuous sleep. The waking is ancestral. What makes it torment is the panic, the conviction that something is broken, which is exactly the kind of conviction you can only have in a world where nobody has ever heard of the watch. Some sleep therapists now tell their patients the quietly radical thing: lying peacefully awake in the middle of the night is not failure. It is, historically, normal.

But the larger thing that ended was not a sleep schedule. It was a country.

Consider what happened to the price of light. In the ancient world, an hour of lamplight cost a day's wages, by one estimate; today an hour of bright light costs a fraction of a second of an average one. We did not merely buy more light than our ancestors. We bought the abolition of night as an institution, the same way certain technologies abolished distance. Look at the NASA composites, the Earth at night, Europe's coastline drawn in gold thread, and you are looking at a map of wealth and power as legible as any atlas: the Korean peninsula at night shows the south as a constellation and the north as an absence, a darkness with one small spark where Pyongyang is. Light is money and order. Darkness is whatever is left.

And the sky itself has been paying. A landmark study found that more than eighty percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies, and that the Milky Way is hidden from three out of five Europeans and roughly four out of five North Americans. Worse, it is getting worse: one recent analysis of citizen observations found the night sky brightening by nearly ten percent a year, a rate at which the stars you can see halve within a decade. The single best anecdote about all this comes from the Northridge earthquake, which struck Los Angeles at 4:30 in the morning in January 1994 and knocked out power across the city. In the sudden dark, residents began calling the police and the Griffith Observatory to report an alarming phenomenon, a vast, strange, silvery cloud hanging over the blacked-out hills. It was the Milky Way. People were calling emergency services about their own galaxy, because it had appeared where it had no right to appear, over a city where it had not been visible in living memory.

The cruelty of it is that nobody chose this. Every porch light is rational. Every car dealership's floodlit lot is somebody's livelihood. The abolition of night is a tragedy of the commons written in photons, and it is also, in one narrow sense, the most forgiving pollution on Earth: unlike mercury or carbon, light leaves no residue at all. Turn it off, and the dark comes back complete, as if nothing had ever happened.

Meanwhile the dark was doing more work than we knew. It was not an absence but an instruction. The body reads light at all times; melatonin flows only in darkness; the WHO's cancer agency has classified night-shift work involving circadian disruption as a probable human carcinogen, which is a clinical way of saying that the night shift is an exposure, like asbestos with better lighting. And the dark was habitat. Sea turtle hatchlings orient toward the brighter horizon, which for a hundred million years meant the sea and its reflected sky; today they crawl inland toward the sodium glow of a beachfront road, and volunteers in Florida spend their nights flipping them around. Moths may steer by keeping their backs toward what they take for the sky, which is a sensible navigation trick until the sky is a streetlight and up is down; they spiral in until they die or are eaten, their oldest instinct used against them. Fireflies flash their courtship into a glare that answers nothing. Hundreds of millions of birds die each year colliding with buildings in North America, many drawn off course by the glitter of cities they mistake for something navigable. Even trees are confused; streetlit ones hold their leaves longer, unwilling to accept that summer is over. The dark was a biome. We are demolishing it at the speed of development, and since it belongs to no one, no one is its keeper.

Here is the part I find hardest to get over. You cannot see the stars in daylight. Not because they are gone; they are there at noon exactly as at midnight, pouring across the sky while you eat lunch. Daylight doesn't remove them. It drowns them. Darkness is not the opposite of light but its medium, the one register in which faint things become real. Your eyes know this: in the dark they spend half an hour building their instrument, and then whole galaxies are available. The oldest sky-readers on Earth took the point literally. Aboriginal Australian astronomers chart constellations made not of stars but of darkness itself, the Emu in the Sky drawn in the black dust lanes beside the river of the Milky Way; the Inca saw a llama and a fox in the shadow-clouds between the stars. There are figures you can only see in the dark, and they vanish first.

I would not push the metaphor too far, but I notice that it keeps being true. Most of what matters in a life is faint. Grief is faint. Memory is faint. Other people's inner lives are faint, and so is your own when you finally get quiet enough to hear it. These things show best in unlit hours: the drive home, the long wait, the middle of the night when the whole bright apparatus of the day is switched off and something small and true comes up like a star. We have gotten very good at medicating such hours with feeds and noise, and I include myself, but it is worth being honest about what the treatment costs. A world that is fully lit all the time is a world in which only the bright things are permitted to be real.

None of this is an argument against light. Let me be clear about that, because the temptation to romanticize is strong and the truth is not romantic. Pre-electric night was cold, and frightening, and it killed people: the fever that turned bad overnight, the fire in the thatch, the childbirth with no lamp bright enough to help. Artificial light is one of the plainest, least complicated goods in the entire human story. The surgeon's lamp. The light left on for someone coming home late. The woman reading after her children sleep, the first women in history free to do so. No one should have to live in the old dark. The argument is only against thoughtlessness, against totality, against the assumption that because a little light is good, all light is better.

And there are already people keeping the dark on purpose, the way we keep wilderness. Flagstaff, Arizona, passed the first municipal lighting ordinance in 1958, not out of sentiment but to protect the sky over Lowell Observatory, where Pluto had been found twenty-eight years before; the city has been quarreling gracefully with its own glow ever since. There are dark-sky reserves now on four continents, places where the night is managed like a fishery or a forest. The tools are almost comically modest: fixtures that aim down, bulbs that glow amber instead of blue-white, motion sensors so that light exists when it is needed and not otherwise, curfews. That last word deserves its second life. The first curfew told households to bank their fires. A new curfew would tell a city to bank its glow, and unlike nearly every other repair we owe the natural world, this one completes itself instantly, the moment we switch it off.

We are the first generations who could give the night away entirely, and therefore the first who have to choose it. I think about that choice as a small human moment rather than a large planetary one: a child, somewhere the power has failed or the family has driven far enough, standing outside past bedtime, looking up, and asking what that cloud is, and being told: that is not a cloud. That is the galaxy we live in. You are looking at the inside of your own home.

Night is not what is left over when the day is finished. It is the other half of everything. It is still there, entire and waiting, a few hours' drive from almost anywhere. The dark is a country, and it has never actually been conquered, only occupied. Whether it passes to our children whole or in ruins is a decision that gets made one porch light at a time, and it is still, unlike so many decisions now, entirely ours to make.
