# The Country of Night

In January 1994, an earthquake struck Los Angeles in the dark hours of the morning and knocked out power across most of the city. Residents came out of their houses and looked up at a sky none of them recognized, and some of them called 911, and some called the Griffith Observatory, to ask about an enormous, ominous, silvery cloud hanging over the streets. The cloud was the Milky Way. Many of the callers had lived their entire lives beneath it without once seeing it.

I think about those phone calls often. They hold a parable in miniature. We have altered the night so thoroughly, and so quickly, that most of us have forgotten what it is — have gone, in a historical eyeblink, from being creatures of the dark to creatures who visit the dark, briefly, through a window. Night is half of everything. The Earth spends half of every rotation turned away from the sun, and for all but the last century of our species' existence, we spent that half in a darkness modern people have never once experienced. What follows is an attempt to remember what that half was like: what the night used to be, what we built in its place, and what — this is the hopeful part — is still recoverable, with a switch.

Begin with the basics. For almost the entire human story, night was genuinely dark. Not dim — dark. There was no glow on the horizon from a town over the hill, because there was no glow. Under a new moon in open country you could not see your hand in front of your face. Travelers got lost between villages a mile apart. The moon was the only streetlamp, and it kept an eccentric schedule. Light was the exception and the expense — expensive in treasure, expensive in danger, since keeping flame alive inside a house of thatch and timber was always a small gamble with everyone's life.

Because night was genuinely dangerous, our ancestors organized against it. The word *curfew* comes from the French *couvre-feu*: cover the fire. In medieval towns a bell rang at a fixed hour ordering every hearth banked — a city of wooden roofs collectively exhaling its flames so it could sleep without burning down. In London you could hire a link-boy, a child with a flaming torch, to walk you home through streets that had no public light at all. The night had its own jurisdiction. Thieves and smugglers used it; so did ghosts, demons, and the restless dead; folklore assigned the hours after midnight to spirits and the hours before dawn to melancholy. Darkness wasn't an aesthetic. It was a weather system, and people dressed for it.

Yet the historians of night keep returning to something else: the darkness was also furnished with intimacy. Families slept in shared beds for warmth, packed in with visitors and apprentices and strangers off the road. Conversation in the dark has a candor daylight doesn't allow — when nobody can see anyone, something loosens. Firelight was the gathering point; storytelling was the entertainment; the night functioned less as the day's enemy than as its annex, a second room in the house of the world.

There is an economic way to see how recently all this changed. An economist named William Nordhaus once spent years doing something that sounds absurd and turned out to be illuminating in both senses: pricing light across history. His finding, roughly: for most of human history, an hour of reading by lamp cost the better part of a day's wage. In some ancient reckonings, an hour of oil-lamp light cost days of labor. Today an hour of electric light costs a fraction of a second of median earnings. When you hear that darkness ruled most of human life, understand it as a matter of budget. The night reigned because light was unaffordable. We did not so much abolish the night as make it cheap to ignore.

In 2005, the historian Roger Ekirch published *At Day's Close*, a history of night in the pre-industrial West, built from years spent in diaries, letters, court records, sermons, and medical texts. Reading through them, he kept tripping over a phrase: *first sleep*. It appears in English, in French (*premier sommeil*), in Italian (*primo sonno*), across two millennia, always in the tone people use for things that everyone knows. First sleep was the sleep you took when you went to bed not long after dark. You slept hard, deeply, for three or four hours. Then, around midnight, you woke — not with a jolt, but naturally, gently, into a calm interlude that contemporaries called *the watch*, which might last an hour or more.

People did things in the watch. They got up and tended the fire, prayed, talked, smoked a pipe, checked on the livestock, gossiped with neighbors who were also awake, made love — the physicians of the era actually recommended the interval as the best time for conception — or simply lay still and thought, with no daylight errands left to dilute the thinking. Then they went back down into second sleep until dawn.

For a long time this looked like mere custom. Then in the 1990s, Thomas Wehr, a sleep researcher at the National Institute of Mental Health, ran what amounted to an attempt to retrieve the old night in a laboratory. He gave volunteers fourteen hours of darkness each night for a month — a clinical winter. After an adjustment period, the subjects did something remarkable: their sleep split. They slept in two blocks, waking after midnight into a quiet, dreamy, distinctly pleasant wakefulness — prolactin rising, the body settling into a mode no one had a name for — and then slept again until morning. The pattern Ekirch had found in five centuries of documents reappeared the moment darkness was returned to it. Bimodal sleep looks less like a habit we once had and more like a setting we lost.

Which casts a strange, tender light on a modern complaint. Waking at 3 a.m. and finding ourselves awake, unable to sink back down, we call it insomnia and treat it as a malfunction. It may be an echo — the watch arriving punctually in a world no longer shaped to receive it. The hour may not be broken. The schedule around it is.

The machines that ended the night arrived fast. Gaslight appeared on London's Pall Mall in 1807; within a few decades, tens of thousands of burners glowed in London and Paris, and the lamplighter with his long pole became a fixture of dusk — a moving constellation at eye level. Then came electricity: arc lamps like small captive suns in the 1870s and 80s, then Edison's filaments. By 1900, the night — the oldest human condition, older than language, older than fire's domestication — had been converted into an infrastructure problem with a solution.

What artificial light actually invented was the evening. Before it, the hours after dark belonged to rest, talk, and courtship by candle. After it, they became a market: theaters, cafés, dance halls, cinemas, restaurants, the glittering secondary life of cities that now runs from seven at night until two in the morning. The city that never sleeps stopped being a boast and became a specification.

The cost was absorbed by a workforce most of us never see. Walk through any city at four in the morning and you will find it inhabited: bakers shaping loaves in yellow light, nurses on their rounds, stocking crews wheeling pallets, controllers watching blips, the technicians who keep the water pumping and the servers humming, drivers on their second coffee. Millions of people — in industrialized countries, as many as one in five workers — labor while the rest of us sleep, an invisible crew our comfort floats on. In 2007, the World Health Organization's cancer research agency did something quiet and remarkable: it classified shift work involving circadian disruption as a probable human carcinogen. Night, once merely frightening, now has a mortality schedule.

And then there is the sky itself. In 2016, an international team led by the physicist Fabio Falchi published the first complete atlas of artificial sky brightness. Its numbers deserve to be sat with for a moment. More than 80 percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies. For a third of humanity, the Milky Way is invisible. In Europe, roughly 60 percent of people cannot see it; in North America, about 80 percent cannot. Look at the Earth from orbit at night — NASA's composite images render civilization as a lace of light strung along coastlines and rivers — and you are looking at something genuinely beautiful that is also, in a sense, exhaust: light escaping upward, scattering off the atmosphere into a luminous dome, a *skyglow* detectable from a hundred miles away.

Living things swim in that exhaust. For centuries, "like a moth to a flame" implied desire. Slow-motion cameras have shown something stranger: insects instinctively tilt their backs toward the brightest point in view, a reflex calibrated to keep them upright beneath an open sky with the moon as a steady reference overhead. Around a porch light, the reflex becomes a doom-loop. They circle not because they love the light but because their bodies are convinced it is the sky.

Migrating birds steer by starlight and the earth's glow, and city lights pull them off course; collisions with buildings kill as many as a billion birds a year in the United States. The Tribute in Light over Manhattan after September 11 — two towers of pure vertical brightness — turned out to be an accidental experiment: migrating birds gathered in orbit inside the beams at extraordinary densities, and when researchers persuaded the organizers to douse the lights for twenty minutes, the birds dispersed almost immediately. The machinery of their confusion simply switched off. Sea turtle hatchlings, emerging at night on a beach, orient toward the brighter horizon — on a wild coast that is moonlight on water; on a developed one, it is a resort — and Florida towns now pass lighting ordinances every hatching season so that hatchlings find the ocean instead of the parking lot. Even plants feel it: a Swiss study found that meadow plots lit by ordinary LED lamps at night received nearly two-thirds fewer visits from pollinating insects, and set less fruit. Night is not empty. Darkness is not the absence of habitat; it *is* habitat, for a vast fraction of the living world, and we have been paving it the way we pave wetlands — without quite noticing, because it doesn't look like anything.

And what of the mind in all this? The 3 a.m. brain has its reputation for a reason. Partly it is mechanics: the prefrontal cortex is tired, no news arrives, no errands interrupt, no one is awake to reality-check you, and rumination gets the whole room. Anxieties that daylight dilutes concentrate in the dark like sediment in a glass. Every insomniac knows the special physics of the 3 a.m. problem: it is always larger at night, and by morning it has shrunk back to size, as though daylight were a solvent.

But night also does stranger, kinder work. Mary Shelley was eighteen in 1816, the year without a summer, holed up on Lake Geneva with Byron and a dare to write ghost stories, when she fell into what she called a waking dream — the pale student, the thing stirring on the table — that became *Frankenstein*. Kekulé claimed the ring structure of benzene came to him as a dream of a snake seizing its own tail. The unconscious keeps the night shift. It takes the problems we fall asleep holding and returns them rearranged by morning. Night thought is not defective day thought; it is a different instrument — looser, less defended — and some of what our species has made appeared first in that other room.

Here is the good news, and it is rare enough in environmental news of any kind: this particular damage reverses at the speed of a switch. Air and water pollution take decades and fortunes to undo. Light pollution ends when the light ends. The dark-sky movement has mapped this out in practice. Central Idaho holds a certified dark sky reserve the size of a small country. On the Isle of Coll, off Scotland, an entire community agreed to manage its lighting so that visitors can see the Milky Way from the football pitch. Tucson, Arizona, sits within sight of some of the world's great observatories, and decades ago the city rewrote its lighting code — full shielding, warm bulbs, light aimed at the ground where it is useful instead of the sky where it isn't — and the observatories kept their view. None of these places is poorer for it. They simply buy their light the way our ancestors had to: on purpose.

And at the scale of a single evening: it takes about twenty minutes of true darkness for human eyes to reach full sensitivity — a dilation you can feel happening, the world quietly assembling itself out of fainter and fainter signals. Guides at dark-sky parks report a curious thing: visitors who see the Milky Way for the first time go silent, and some of them weep. Not only, I think, at the beauty of it — a river of several hundred billion suns, visible to the naked eye — but at the return of something. Gratitude and grief feel similar at first.

Which brings us back to Los Angeles in 1994. The silvery cloud over the blacked-out city had been there the whole time — above the traffic, above the billboards, the whole time. It took a catastrophe to show people what they had, in effect, turned off. There is a version of that blackout available in miniature, any night, anywhere. Our ancestors woke in the watch and lay in the dark between first sleep and second sleep, unbothered, watching embers, thinking their long thoughts, sometimes stepping outside into a sky absolutely stiff with stars. Some of us still wake in that hour and reach, first thing, for a small bright screen — colonizing the last of the night even from bed. But the wakefulness might be read another way: not as a malfunction, but as punctuality. The night was never the other half of the world. It is the half we came from, and it is still there, patient, just above the streetlights, waiting for the switch.

# Losing the Night

At 4:31 on the morning of January 17, 1994, an earthquake measuring 6.7 struck beneath the San Fernando Valley, snapping power lines and plunging Los Angeles into sudden darkness. In the eerie quiet after the shaking stopped, residents who stumbled outside saw something vast and faint arched over the city: a river of pale light, dusted with grain, running horizon to horizon. According to astronomers at the Griffith Observatory, the phones started ringing. Callers wanted to know what the giant silvery cloud was, and whether it posed any danger. It was the Milky Way—the galaxy we live inside, viewed edge-on from within—a sight every human being had shared for a hundred thousand years, and which many Angelenos had somehow never had.

The anecdote usually gets told as a joke about clueless city people. It isn't funny. It's a report from a crime scene. Something was taken—quietly, fixture by fixture, decade by decade—and the theft was so complete that its victims didn't know what they'd been robbed of. They looked up into a hole in the sky and, not knowing it was a hole, called it a cloud.

For nearly the entire history of our species, night meant real darkness. Not the dim darkness of a modern suburb, where the sky never quite goes black, but darkness that fell like a verdict: darkness in which the landscape disappeared and the sky became the brightest thing in the world. Under those conditions, the stars were not decoration. They were infrastructure. The Milky Way was the single most conspicuous object in the night of every human who ever lived until roughly the era of our grandparents. Every culture named it. The Greeks saw Hera's spilled milk and gave us the word *galaxy* from it. Chinese astronomers called it the Silver River, separating the star of the Weaver Girl from her Cowherd on opposite banks. The San people of the Kalahari called it the Backbone of Night. And some Aboriginal Australian nations read the dark rifts running along the Milky Way's length as an Emu in the Sky—a constellation made not of stars but of shadow itself, a figure drawn in the negative space. Under skies we no longer have, observers swear the Milky Way is bright enough to cast a faint shadow of its own.

From that river of light, humanity built its first sciences. Astronomy is the oldest of them for a reason: the sky was the original clock, calendar, and scripture. The moon's phases gave us the month. The wandering planets and the wheel of constellations gave us the year and its festivals. Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of open ocean reading the rising and setting points of stars, holding entire continents of knowledge in memory. The date of Easter still hides a full moon inside it; Ramadan still begins with a sighting. We are, all of us, descended from people who knew the night sky the way modern city dwellers know traffic signals.

Darkness shaped not just our cultures but our bodies. The historian Roger Ekirch, combing diaries, court records, medical texts, and prayer books from the preindustrial world, discovered something strange: for centuries, Western sleep came in two acts. People went to bed shortly after dark, slept deeply for three or four hours—the "first sleep"—then woke naturally around midnight and stayed awake for an hour or so before returning to the "second sleep." The interval had a name in dozens of languages: French *premier sommeil*, Italian *primo sonno*. It was a recognized hour of its own, used for prayer, for reflecting on dreams, for talking quietly by the fire, for making love. Court records even capture burglars plying their trade in the gap between sleeps. The word *midnight* makes sense only in a world where night had a middle you were sometimes awake to see.

The sleep researcher Thomas Wehr later ran an experiment that amounts to an archaeology of the body. He gave volunteers fourteen hours of darkness every night for a month—mimicking the light schedule of a winter in a preindustrial world—and their sleep quietly reorganized itself into the old pattern: a block of deep sleep, a calm and contemplative hour of wakefulness, another block of sleep. The hour between wasn't insomnia. It looked like a feature, something the body does when the dark lasts long enough. We didn't merely lose the night. We changed what sleep is.

Then we lit the world. In 1807, London's Pall Mall became one of the first streets anywhere glowing with gaslight; before that, the desperate hired linkboys—children with flaming torches—to walk them home through the black. Paris, the so-called City of Light, blazed next. Edison's Pearl Street station switched on lower Manhattan in 1882. And after the Second World War, cheap electricity met cheap fixtures and the flood began in earnest: billboards, ballparks, strip malls, stadiums, parking lots lit like operating theaters at 2 a.m.

The result is measured by satellites, which is its own dark joke—the view of our lights from space is now better than our view of the stars from the ground. The 2016 world atlas of artificial night sky brightness found that more than 80 percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies; in the United States and Europe, it's 99 percent. About a third of all people alive—including roughly 80 percent of North Americans—cannot see the Milky Way from where they live. And it's accelerating. A 2023 study drawing on a decade of citizen-scientist star counts concluded that skyglow is brightening about 9.6 percent per year. The authors put it in human terms: a child born where 250 stars are visible tonight would see only about 100 from the same spot by their eighteenth birthday.

The culprit is mostly *skyglow*—light thrown upward or sideways that scatters off air and aerosols and returns as a luminous fog. Stand on a ridge a hundred miles from a major city on a clear night and you can still see its dome, a pale blister on the horizon, the ghost of a million bad fixtures. Add glare, light trespass, and clutter, and you have the full catastrophe: not darkness's absence but its occupation.

We lit the world without asking what the darkness was for. Other species hadn't finished answering either. Consider the sea turtle, whose hatchlings emerge from the sand on Florida beaches and instinctively race toward the brightest horizon—which, for a hundred million years, meant the moonlit sea. Now it often means a strip mall behind the dunes, and thousands of hatchlings a year march inland to die on highways and in pools. Towns that darken their beaches during nesting season watch the hatchlings find the water again. Consider the September 11 Tribute in Light in Manhattan, whose twin beams turned out to be an unplanned ecological experiment: researchers estimated the beams trapped more than a million migrating birds across the nights studied—songbirds circling in the light like moths, burning fuel they needed to fly on. The organizers now switch the beams off for about twenty minutes at a stretch whenever monitoring shows large numbers of birds circling, and the birds pour out of the beams and resume their journey. Consider the insects: a British study found that streetlights cut caterpillar numbers in hedgerows roughly in half, and moths—the night's great pollinators—are lured into streetlights to circle until they die of exhaustion or predation. Fireflies court with light, and we have drowned the conversation. Even coral reefs sense the moon: spawning is synchronized to its cycle, and experiments show that artificial night light can scramble the timing, desynchronizing an event that depends on every reef doing it at once.

We're not exempt. Nighttime light suppresses melatonin, and blue-rich white LEDs—the kind we've blanketed the world in over the past decade—are the most potent kind. The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies shift work involving circadian disruption as probably carcinogenic to humans. Chronic exposure to light at night is linked to sleep disorders, metabolic disease, depression. We took a rhythm our bodies kept for a hundred thousand years and broke it in three generations.

None of this is an argument for a world of darkness, and honesty requires saying so. Light at night is a genuine good: it means safety, emergency rooms, the teenager walking home, the simple pleasure of a lit street. The problem is not light. The problem is waste and thoughtlessness—light that spills where it does no good, aimed where nothing needs seeing, burning all night where no one is awake. By some estimates, a third of outdoor lighting in the United States is thrown straight into the sky, at a cost of billions of dollars a year, illuminating nothing but air. And the safety argument for that waste is weaker than it looks. When English councils switched off or dimmed streetlights in natural experiments across dozens of areas, researchers found no significant increase in crime or traffic accidents. Meanwhile, poorly designed lighting can make things worse: an overlit parking lot creates glare that blinds you to everything outside the beam, and blacker shadows at its edges. Good lighting, it turns out, is not more light. It's shielded, warm-colored, aimed at the ground, and off when nobody needs it.

Here is what moves me most about all of this: the loss was never chosen, and the reversal costs almost nothing. No parliament ever voted to remove the Milky Way from the sky. It vanished as an externality, accumulating one unshielded fixture at a time, each decision individually reasonable—a safer parking lot, a brighter storefront—while the sum of all of them erased the oldest shared experience of our species. Every environmental loss we usually mourn has the same shape and a terrible asymmetry: the carbon takes centuries to recapture, the extinct species never comes back, the ozone hole closes on the scale of decades. Skyglow heals at the speed of a light switch. The moment the lights come down—or are aimed down—the sky above any town returns to something like what it was for Galileo. Of all the wounds we've inflicted on the natural world, this is the only one that closes overnight. We polluted the night with something as easy to stop as light. There is something both comic and consoling in that, and more than a little shaming: the stars are not gone. They are merely hidden behind our carelessness, and carelessness is reversible.

Which is why the hope here is more than rhetoric. Flagstaff, Arizona—protecting the observatory where Pluto was discovered—passed America's first lighting ordinance in 1958 and became the world's first certified Dark Sky City in 2001. More than two hundred places worldwide, from Aoraki Mackenzie in New Zealand to entire counties in the American Southwest, have earned Dark Sky certification by shielding fixtures, capping brightness, and embracing curfews. France now requires most non-essential shop and office lights to go out overnight. Amber, full-cutoff lighting lets Florida hatchlings find the sea. Even the pandemic, for all its horror, gave a glimpse: with traffic stilled, skyglow measurably thinned, and there are photographs from locked-down cities of Venus blazing over empty avenues. The barrier was never technological. It's attention. Nobody misses a night sky they've never seen; each generation's baseline quietly erodes, the way we stopped missing quiet when we stopped hearing it.

So here is the whole prescription, or the beginning of one: go find out what was stolen. Drive an hour or two beyond the glow of any city, on a clear moonless night, and then wait—this is the crucial part, and the hard one—because your eyes need the better part of half an hour to adapt, and a single glance at a phone screen will undo most of it. Stand in a field. Let the darkness become total. And then look up.

What you will see first is not faintness but abundance, a shock of it: the Milky Way not as a smudge but as a structure, a luminous river with dark channels running through it, so bright it seems it should hum. You are seeing the disk of your own galaxy from the inside, from the outskirts of an unremarkable spiral arm, light from a hundred billion suns arriving all at once across distances your brain will refuse to convert into miles. Every person you've read about in a history book saw this. Every one of them. It was the common inheritance of every human being who ever lived, and you have to drive two hours and switch off your phone to collect it.

The stars did not go out. They are exactly where they have always been, waiting behind the glare, patient in a way that shames us. Last time Los Angeles saw them, it took an earthquake to turn out the lights. It shouldn't take one next time. The darkness isn't the enemy, and never was—it's the backdrop against which the whole human story happened, the canvas under which we learned to keep time, tell stories, and wonder what we were. It costs nothing to give it back. The stars only ask that we stop shining so much at the ground, and look up.

# What the Eel Knows

There is a fact I have trouble holding in my head, and I'd like to hand it to you while it's fresh: no human being has ever seen two eels mate.

Sit with that a moment. We have filmed giant squid in the abyss and snow leopards in the Himalaya. We have landed a robot on a comet and watched, in real time, a whale deliver a calf. We can sequence the genome of anything that holds still, and of plenty of things that don't. And yet the European eel, an animal so ordinary that it turns up in garden ponds and drainage ditches and buckets outside bait shops, has never once, in the entire history of human observation, been caught in the act of reproduction. Not in the wild. Not in an aquarium, where eels have been kept for more than a century and have refused, always, to spawn the natural way. The most ordinary act of its existence has been performed, by now, some unimaginable trillions of times, and witnessed by no one.

For most of history this was not a charming curiosity. It was an embarrassment. Every other animal has parents. Chickens come from eggs laid by chickens. Mayflies hatch from rivers in which you can find their larvae. The eel, by contrast, simply appeared, each spring, in rivers across Europe, with no visible origin and no visible means of production. It arrived after heavy rains, sometimes crossing wet meadows on damp nights, nosing over grass and stone as if it were condensing out of the dew itself. Medieval naturalists weren't sure whether it was a fish or a serpent, and some declined to eat it on the grounds that its origins were, in the strictest sense, unknowable.

The eel has been getting away with this for as long as there have been people to notice.

What we actually know about the eel's life reads less like biology than like a cold case file, assembled from circumstantial evidence over thousands of years. Here is the reconstruction, as best we can make it: European eels are born, presumably, in a region of open ocean called the Sargasso Sea, a shoreless stretch of warm water east of Bermuda. From there, the newborn larvae drift for one to three years across the entire Atlantic, riding the Gulf Stream, until they arrive at the coasts of Europe as glass eels, creatures the size of a fingernail and about as transparent. They darken, wriggle upstream, and spend the next ten, twenty, forty years in freshwater as yellow eels. Then, when some interior clock strikes, they transform again: they turn silver, their eyes enlarge, their digestive tracts begin to dissolve, and they stop eating entirely. Swimming on stored fat alone, they travel five thousand kilometers or more back to the Sargasso, spawn once, and presumably die.

This means that every European eel you have ever seen crossed an ocean as an infant. The one in your garden pond. The ones in the Seine, the Thames, the Danube. It is as if someone told you, with a straight face, that every sparrow in London hatched in the middle of the Pacific.

For a long time, nobody bought it. Aristotle examined the question and concluded, reasonably enough given what he could see, that eels sprang spontaneously from the mud of riverbeds, generated from what he called the entrails of the earth, with neither egg nor copulation involved. Pliny the Elder offered that adult eels reproduce by scraping themselves against rocks, the scrapings coming alive. Folk tradition across Europe held that eels were born of horsehairs fallen into water, a belief so persistent that it took actual science to untangle it: certain hairworms really do seem to materialize from horse troughs, having completed their strange lives inside insects, and the confusion was almost forgivable. The eel's problem was that it offered no evidence of anything. A freshwater eel has no visible gonads. It is, for most of its life, effectively prepubescent, a creature whose sexuality is deferred until the journey it takes in secret, at the end of which it is beyond our reach. It outlasted every theory about itself by simply declining to be caught at it.

Which brings us, improbably, to Sigmund Freud.

In 1876, Freud was a nineteen-year-old medical student in Vienna, and his professor assigned him a research trip to Trieste with a specific mission: dissect eels and find the testes. This was, at the time, a genuine open question of comparative anatomy. Freud spent roughly four months at the zoological station, working through some four hundred eels, knife in hand, looking for the answer to where eels come from. He found, in a few specimens, tissue he took to be immature sexual organs, published a small, cautious paper, and admitted that the material at hand could not settle the matter. The mature male eel eluded him; eels mature only on that secret journey he could not follow. He left Trieste, left the eels, and went on to a career built on the conviction that nothing hidden stays hidden forever, that every symptom has a source, that if you dig deeply enough you will find the organ of the matter. The first great mystery he failed to solve was, fittingly, sex. One imagines four hundred eels, each one interrogated at length, each one refusing to say a word.

The eel's baby had been hiding in plain sight for a century before anyone connected the dots. Naturalists had long known of a creature called the leptocephalus: a flat, transparent thing shaped like a willow leaf, so clear you could see straight through its body, which moved through the sea with a strange sideways flutter. It was described and named in the eighteenth century as its own genus, its own species, its own kind of animal, because it looked nothing whatsoever like an eel. Only in the 1890s, when two Italian zoologists raised the larvae through metamorphosis in tanks at Messina, was it established beyond doubt that the leaf was the child. The eel does not merely grow up. It becomes, over its life, several different animals wearing one another's skin.

The man who finally cornered the secret was a Dane named Johannes Schmidt, and he went at the problem like a detective reconstructing a crime from scuff marks. His logic was elegant: larval eels grow as they drift, so if you catch them everywhere in the ocean and measure them, the smallest ones, the youngest ones, will point you toward the cradle. From 1904 onward, funded in part by Danish beer money through the Carlsberg Foundation, Schmidt trawled the Atlantic with fine-mesh nets, for nearly two decades, pausing for the First World War, counting and measuring larvae by the thousand. The map converged slowly, like a shy witness eventually pointing west, then southwest. In the early 1920s he could announce it: the smallest larvae, just a few millimeters long, came from the Sargasso Sea, that vast, uncanny region bounded not by land but by currents, carpeted with drifting sargassum weed, sitting in the windless horse latitudes that old sailors associated with becalmed ships and rotting crews. The spawning ground of every eel in every European river turned out to be closer to New York than to Lisbon.

Even now, with Schmidt's map a century old, the strangeness has not worn off, and the case is not closed. No one has ever observed eels spawning in the Sargasso or anywhere else. No one has ever collected a fertilized European eel egg from the open sea; the smallest larvae are the earliest evidence anyone has found. For decades, not a single adult eel was ever caught in the open Atlantic mid-journey. Only in recent years have satellite tags followed migrating eels into Sargasso waters, and even then the tags mostly surfaced on their own, reporting positions after the fact. What data we have suggest the eels spend their days diving to depths of several hundred meters and rising again at night, for reasons nobody understands. In captivity, researchers have coaxed eels to spawn only through hormone injections, and the larvae rarely survive more than a few days. The life cycle has never been closed. Which means that every farmed eel on Earth, in every aquaculture facility from Japan to Madagascar, began as a wild-caught baby. We can grow eels, but we cannot make them. The last open question of eel biology happens to be the choke point of eel conservation, and nobody planned it that way.

The eel, meanwhile, plays by its own rules, and the rules are strange. Its sex is not fixed at conception but negotiated with its circumstances: crowded waters produce males, spacious waters produce females, as if the eel were checking the neighborhood before deciding what to be. Its puberty can be postponed for decades. There was, until 2014, an eel in a well in the village of Brantevik, in southern Sweden, reportedly thrown into the well as a glass eel in 1859, that lived to be about a hundred and fifty-five years old, outlasting the American Civil War, two world wars, and several successive generations of the family that kept it. Wells full of eels were once a working tradition across northern Europe: a living larder in the backyard, and, if the stories are to be believed, something like a companion. In Māori tradition, the great longfin eels are taonga, treasures; some were regarded as guardians of specific places, beings you did not simply catch but negotiated with. An animal that breathes through its skin, climbs damp stone, and crosses dewy meadows at night makes a better neighbor than a fish.

Which is what makes the last chapter so hard to write. Since the late 1970s, the number of glass eels arriving in Europe has fallen by something like ninety to ninety-five percent. The European eel is listed as critically endangered. The causes appear to be stacked, a casino of bad luck: dams and hydroelectric turbines that kill migrants in both directions, habitat loss, pollution, shifting currents in the spawning grounds themselves, and a parasitic worm from East Asia that hitchhiked in imported eels in the 1980s and now inflames their swim bladders, possibly ruining their buoyancy for exactly the crossing their lives are built around. We may have broken their road home before we ever knew where home was.

And then there is the market. Baby eels are called white gold for a reason; at their peak they have sold for over a thousand euros a kilogram, flown live to Asia to stock farms, smuggled by the ton in luggage and shipping containers in a black market that Europol pursues across borders. In the Basque Country, a plate of true elvers has become so expensive that restaurants serve gulas, a counterfeit made of surimi pressed into the shape of baby eels. Spain now eats an imitation of a mystery.

There is something almost tender in the countermeasures. In New Zealand and Sweden, conservationists net migrating adult eels at dams and drive them, by truck, around the turbines to the sea. Human beings ferrying eels to their weddings because we paved over the road they would have walked.

Rachel Carson understood the shape of this story early. Her first book opens by following a silver eel named Anguilla out of her coastal pool, down the river, and across the Atlantic toward the Sargasso, and you can feel in it the recognition that the eel's life is fundamentally a homecoming, a return to a place it has never seen. I think about the eel more than is probably reasonable, and what stays with me is this: it kept its secret through Aristotle and the fall of Rome, through Freud's four hundred scalpels and Schmidt's twenty years of trawling. It survived every theory ever written about it. And now the secret risks being retired unopened, not solved but orphaned, its only keeper slipping away.

Every other animal eventually told us where babies come from. The eel is the last holdout, the sole confidant of its own origin, and I find I want that secret to survive even unconfessed. Somewhere tonight, a glass eel smaller than a thumbnail is nosing up a dark river, transparent enough to see the stones through, carrying somewhere in its body the answer to a question humans have been asking for two and a half thousand years. I hope it makes it. I hope nobody ever needs a scan to know what's inside it. Some things should stay one step ahead of us. But mostly I hope it makes it because the answer only matters if someone is left alive to ask.

# The Blue Dot and the Horizon

There is a particular quality of silence that arrives the moment you realize you are lost. The forest hasn't changed. The street hasn't changed. *You* have changed. The landmarks that were quietly confirming themselves in the background of your attention—the distinctive boulder, the bend that should have bent the other way—suddenly all stop matching the map you've been carrying in your head, and you understand, with a small cold shock, that the map was wrong or the world was, and either way you are now a creature without coordinates. The path you walked in on has become a hypothesis. The sun, which was scenery a minute ago, is suddenly a witness you aren't sure you can trust.

The body knows before the mind admits it. Pulse up, palms damp, that reflexive spin to look back the way you came. Being lost may be one of the oldest fears we have—every child who has ever let go of a parent's hand in a crowd has met it—and it makes sense that we're built to dread it, because every animal that moves must solve the same problem: how to go out and come back.

We are, it turns out, embarrassingly mediocre at this by the standards of the animal kingdom. Consider the desert ant, *Cataglyphis*, which forages on the scorched surface of the Sahara and then marches home in a straight line across terrain with no landmarks at all. It manages this with a built-in pedometer, counting its strides, and a compass that tracks the sun's polarization. Biologists proved the pedometer by gluing tiny stilts to the ants' legs; the homing ants then overshot their nests by exactly the extra length of their new stride. An insect with a brain of a quarter million neurons carries a functioning odometer, a solar compass, and a memory of distance. Humans needed clocks, star tables, and several centuries of applied mathematics to do worse.

And yet—the species that can barely find its way across a dark room without a trail of breadcrumbs is the one that settled the largest and emptiest region on Earth. The Polynesian voyagers, crossing the Pacific in double-hulled canoes, established communities on islands separated by thousands of kilometers of open water, at a time when European sailors still hugged coastlines. They did it deliberately, against the wind much of the way, over centuries, reaching Hawai'i, Rapa Nui, and Aotearoa and tracing the immense triangle between them. The distance from Hawai'i to Tahiti is roughly the distance from Los Angeles to New York, with no land in between.

In 1976, a canoe called *Hōkūleʻa* made that crossing again without instruments, to demonstrate that the ancestors could really have done it. The navigator was Mau Piailug, from the tiny island of Satawal, one of the last masters of a navigational tradition that had survived in Micronesia. Thirty-four days, twenty-four hundred miles, no compass, no watch, no chart. His students went on to train others, and the voyage is now credited with helping revive an entire cultural lineage that colonization had nearly severed.

How did they do it? Not by magic, and not by luck—the knowledge was systematic, teachable, and precise. Navigators memorized a star compass: the horizon divided into houses, each anchored by the rising or setting point of particular stars, so that a chain of stars rising one after another along the same bearing could steer a canoe through a whole night. They read swells the way we read text, distinguishing the long open-ocean rollers from the backwash that bends around an island, feeling interference patterns through the hull while lying on their stomachs. They watched birds. A frigatebird, which cannot land on water, flying toward the horizon at dusk is a signpost: land within a day's sail that way. Noddies and terns commute shorter distances; their direction home is a better fix. They noted how clouds stack over islands the way heat shimmers over pavement. They even read the glow of phosphorescence in their wake. In the Carolinian tradition, a navigator holds the canoe still in his mind and lets an invisible reference island slide beneath one star after another as he proceeds—a moving map, drawn entirely in imagination, updated moment by moment out of accumulated attention.

Other peoples solved the same problem on land with the same intimacy. In parts of Aboriginal Australia, vast stretches of country are navigated by song: the correct order of verses in a songline is the correct order of landmarks along a route, so that singing the land is traveling it, and the map is performed rather than drawn. Inuit travelers read sastrugi—the wind-carved waves of hard snow—as a compass rose written across the tundra, and took direction from consistent winds, the slope of drifted snow, the sound of ice underfoot. Europeans, crossing featureless oceans, developed dead reckoning: the disciplined, humbling art of knowing where you are by keeping track of where you've been. Sailors heaved a wooden chip log overboard and counted knots in a line paying out through a thirty-second sandglass—hence *knots*—and pegged each half-hour's heading and speed onto a traverse board. From thousands of small measurements, they conjured a position out of pure bookkeeping.

The stakes of doing this wrong were monstrous. On a moonless night in October 1707, a returning British fleet misjudged its longitude and drove onto the rocks of the Isles of Scilly. Four ships went down; as many as two thousand sailors drowned, including the admiral, Sir Cloudesley Shovell, who according to legend made it ashore only to be murdered by a woman for his emerald ring. Longitude—east-west position—was the killer, because while latitude falls out of the sky easily (measure the noon sun's height), longitude requires knowing what time it is *somewhere else while you are here*. Parliament offered £20,000, a fortune, for a practical solution. The eventual winner was a Yorkshire carpenter's son named John Harrison, who spent four decades building clocks of almost deranged ingenuity—grasshopper escapements, caged bearings, grids of wooden gears that needed no oil—watches that kept home-time faithfully through months of salt spray and temperature swings. On a transatlantic trial crossing, Harrison's fourth sea watch drifted by seconds while the best astronomical rivals drifted by miles. Longitude, he had proven, was simply time, and time could be carried in a box.

The old art reached its apex, perhaps, in the most desperate navigation ever attempted. In April 1916, Ernest Shackleton and five men left Elephant Island in an open boat, the six-meter *James Caird*, to fetch rescue for a stranded Antarctic expedition. Their target was South Georgia: an island twenty miles wide, eight hundred miles away across the most violent ocean on Earth. For sixteen days of storm, the captain, Frank Worsley, took sights with a sextant from a pitching deck—the kind of observation where a wave through the wrong half of the horizon ruins everything—counted perhaps four usable ones in the whole voyage, and between them trusted his dead reckoning through fog, sleet, and hurricane. They raised South Georgia almost where he reckoned it would be. Think about what that means: a pencil, a watch, a book of tables, and a man's relentless internal arithmetic, holding a thread across eight hundred miles of chaos to a needle in it.

Which brings the story inward, because it turns out that all this time we've been describing a feature of the human brain. London's taxi drivers must pass an examination called the Knowledge—roughly 25,000 streets within six miles of Charing Cross, memorized over three or four grinding years—before they're allowed to ply the world's most demanding cab routes. In 2000, the neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire scanned their brains and found their posterior hippocampi measurably enlarged, swelling with years of navigation like a muscle with work. Soon after, the underlying machinery came to light: John O'Keefe had discovered "place cells," neurons in the rat hippocampus that fire only when the animal is in one specific spot, and May-Britt and Edvard Moser found "grid cells" in the entorhinal cortex, arranged in a hexagonal lattice that tiles space like graph paper. The brain, in other words, contains an actual map, drawn in voltage, a private coordinate system updated as you move. The two discoveries shared the 2014 Nobel Prize.

The strangest part is what else that mapmaking machinery does. Patients with hippocampal damage struggle not only to navigate but to *imagine*—to picture a new scene at all. It now looks as though episodic memory, the film of your past, and mental simulation, the rehearsal of your future, are both built on the scaffolding of spatial navigation. We evolved as creatures who had to find our way, and then discovered we could reuse the route-tracing equipment to revisit yesterday and pre-live tomorrow. Every remembered afternoon is, at bottom, a place you know how to get back to.

Now consider what happens when we outsource the whole enterprise. Your phone knows where you are by talking to a constellation of more than two dozen satellites, each carrying atomic clocks, each broadcasting the time to within nanoseconds; your receiver listens to several at once and solves for position the way one solves a puzzle with the edges of the puzzle being, quite literally, the speed of light. Here is the detail that gets me every time: the satellite clocks run about 38 microseconds per day fast, after you correct for both the slowing effect of their orbital speed and the speeding effect of weaker gravity at their altitude, and if engineers failed to make that correction, GPS would wander by something like ten kilometers a day. Every errand you run rests on general relativity. You navigate by Einstein while listening to a podcast.

But notice what you're looking at while it works. You're not looking at the world; you're looking at a blue dot on a rectangle held in your hand, watching it crawl along a colored line. And studies—Véronique Bohbot's group has done much of this work—suggest that when people navigate by turn-by-turn instruction, the hippocampus largely idles. With practice, that matters: longitudinal research has found that habitual GPS use is associated with declining spatial memory, and we might guess the mechanism from the taxi drivers in reverse. A brain region that isn't asked to make maps stops making them as well. There are two ways to know a city: as a *route*, a bead threaded on a single string, useful only for that one journey, and as a *survey*, an actual territory held in the mind, with a center and an orientation, from which you can improvise any path anywhere. GPS trains the first. It hands you beads on a string and you never have to learn the shape of the necklace.

There is a texture of experience that goes with this. People now arrive in cities and see them as corridors—left here, four hundred meters, then right—moving through them the way a cable moves through a conduit, without ever assembling the place into a whole. The device's voice is calm, authoritative, and sometimes wrong: drivers have followed instructions into rivers, into the desert, into snow. In 2006 a family driving through Oregon followed a road their navigation showed as a shortcut; it was a Forest Service track that became a blizzard-blocked dead end, and the father, leaving the car to find help, never came back. The lesson isn't only about bad maps. It's about what happens to judgment when a calm voice tells you the turn is now. And a map, any map, is at best an argument—simplified, dated, drawn with intentions—while the terrain always gets the final vote.

I don't want to be merely nostalgic, though, because being lost has its own strange gifts, and there's a reason the idea keeps pulling at writers. Rebecca Solnit has written that losing things, and losing your way, can be a beginning rather than a failure. Thoreau put it better in *Walden*: not till we are lost, he says—not till we have lost the world—do we begin to find ourselves, and realize where we are and the infinite extent of our relations. The deliberate wanderer, phone in pocket, knows this: the discovery belongs to the one who strays. The café you remember from every trip is never the one you were walking to. "Lost" is a word that only makes sense against an itinerary. Absent one, you are not lost; you are simply *somewhere*, which is the condition from which every map ever made has started.

Meanwhile the animals continue to humble us. In 2022, a young bar-tailed godwit was tracked flying more than 13,000 kilometers from Alaska to Tasmania without landing—eleven days on the wing, no food, no rest—on a journey it had never made before, somehow holding a course over a featureless ocean. Loggerhead turtles hatch on a Florida beach, crawl into the surf, and decades later navigate the Atlantic in vast loops before returning to nest on the same stretch of sand, apparently reading the Earth's magnetic field like a letter addressed to them. And here is the delicious thing: we still do not fully understand how. A light-sensitive protein in the eye, cryptochrome, may let a robin literally *see* the magnetic field, quantum physics operating in its retina—but the mechanism remains contested. We can put a satellite in orbit so that a teenager can find the nearest bubble tea, and we cannot explain the compass inside a bird.

So the old skills persist in pockets, and it moves me that they do. *Hōkūleʻa* completed a worldwide voyage in the 2010s, navigating by the old methods into dozens of ports, carrying the lesson outward. In London, apprentices still spend years chanting street sequences into tape recorders. Sailing schools teach celestial navigation to people who will never need it, which is of course the point—you learn it the way you learn Latin, to be in conversation with something older than yourself. Orienteering clubs send runners into forests with compasses and the promise that being briefly, safely lost is a sport. And any clear night, anyone can do the oldest thing of all: find the North Star, put your back to it, and know at least this much about where you stand.

What I keep returning to is that knowing where you are was never really about coordinates. Coordinates are what you fall back on when you have no relationship with a place. The Satawal navigator knew where he was the way you know where your own hand is—through contact, through accumulated attention, through being a participant in a world of signs rather than a spectator to a screen. The stars still rise through their houses. The swells still bend around the hidden island and can be felt through a hull. Snow still lies in wind-carved waves that point home. All of it is still legible; we've mostly just stopped reading.

There will be a night, someday, when your phone is dead and the signal is gone and the instructions have run out, and the map you carry inside your skull will be the only one left. On that night you will either have something in your head or you won't. But even before that, on ordinary evenings, it's worth practicing the older stance: leave the blue dot in your pocket, look up until the streetlights drown among the brighter ones, and notice that you are, in fact, somewhere—and that *somewhere* has a shape, and the shape has a north, and the north has always, always been findable by anyone patient enough to stand still and look.

* * *

Lost, the old navigators understood, is just a word for the interval before you pay attention. Pay attention long enough—to swell or sidewalk, star or streetcar bell—and the interval closes. You are found the way they were found: not by a voice telling you to turn right in four hundred meters, but by the slow, quiet restoration of the oldest human friendship, the one between a mind and the ground it moves across. Every map begins there. Every map ends there, too, when the batteries die and the sky is still up, and the stars are still, as they have always been, patiently announcing themselves over a world that was never actually unmapped—only waiting for someone to look.

# A Natural History of the Dark

The night I remember best began with a thunderstorm. I was eight or nine, and sometime after dinner the power died — not with drama but with a small, domestic sound: the refrigerator's hum simply stopped, and I discovered that silence, too, has a shape. My parents lit candles and we sat around the kitchen table playing a card game nobody won, because everyone kept drifting to the windows. Eventually someone stepped onto the front lawn and called the rest of us out. Above the suburban street, above the roofs and the maples, the sky had come undone. Stars everywhere, and across the middle of it a river of faint, grainy light that I had no name for. I didn't know I was looking at the Milky Way, the galaxy we live inside, seen edge-on from the inside. I only knew that it had apparently been there all along, and that the lights hadn't taken the darkness away — they'd been hiding it.

That second part took me years to understand. We tend to treat darkness as a defect of lighting design, an absence we pay a utility company to remove. Flip a switch, banish the void. But darkness is not mere absence. It is a medium, a habitat, an old room of the mind with its own physics, its own ecology, its own long history. Half of everything that happens on this planet happens in the dark, and for most of our species' existence the dark was where we did some of our most important living and thinking. This is a small defense of it: what darkness is, who lives in it, what we were doing in it for a hundred thousand years, and what we've been quietly dismantling since the first electric grids switched on in the 1880s.

Consider the instrument first. The human eye is not one organ but two, stacked in the same orb. Cones handle color and detail and live mostly in the center of your vision; rods handle brightness and live mostly in the periphery. The rods run on a pigment called rhodopsin, which daylight bleaches and darkness slowly rebuilds. This rebuilding takes time — the better part of an hour to reach full night sensitivity. Every time you step from a bright room into the night, you start over. Our ancestors, whose nights were actually night, paid that hour regularly and were paid back with a sky. Most of us never finish the transaction. We step outside under sodium lamps, spend four minutes squinting, and go back in.

There is craft to darkness, and the craft has rules. Look directly at a faint star and it vanishes; look slightly beside it and it reappears, because you've shifted the image onto the rod-rich periphery where the eye's most sensitive detectors live. Under truly dark conditions the eye is absurdly capable. A classic 1942 experiment found that people could perceive flashes containing only a handful of photons — literal quanta of light — and a more recent study suggested that under the right circumstances a single photon striking a single photoreceptor can sometimes reach awareness. There is an old physics-department claim that on a moonless prairie the eye can pick up a candle flame a mile or two away. This is why serious stargazers use red flashlights: the rods are nearly blind to deep red, so a red light lets you read a star chart while your night vision stays intact. Submariners knew the same trick. Darkness rewards patience and punishes impatience, which makes it almost unique among the things we experience.

Night is also a habitat, and its residents are going through something. Sea turtle hatchlings emerge from their nests on moonlit beaches and scramble toward the brighter horizon, which for millions of years meant the sea, moonlight lying on water. Beachfront development inverted the compass. Hatchlings now crawl inland, toward the porch light and the pool deck, and die there by the thousands. The fixes are cheap — amber bulbs, shielded fixtures, lights out during hatching season — and some coastal towns have adopted them, which tells you the problem was never technical.

Or consider the moth at the porch light, that most familiar of summer sights. For centuries the assumption was that moths love light, that they're simply dazzled by it. A 2024 study using high-speed cameras suggested something stranger and sadder: the insects aren't attracted so much as flipped. Many flying insects maintain an ancient reflex called the dorsal light response — they tilt their backs toward whatever is brightest, keeping the sky, the reference frame for level flight, above them. A nearby bulb reads as sky. The moth banks to keep it overhead, overcorrects, banks again, and ends up spiraling around the light in a doomed orbit. Not a moth that can't resist a party. A compass that has been turned inside out.

The dark is also a communications channel, and we are jamming it. Fireflies converse in light — species-specific flash patterns that function as courtship signals — and skyglow drowns their sentences; studies find they flash later, dimmer, or not at all in lit areas. Billions of birds migrate at night, navigating partly by the stars, and artificial light pulls them off course and into glass. Even coral reefs read the night: many corals synchronize their mass spawning to the lunar cycle, releasing eggs and sperm in a coordinated event that depends on the darkness following the full moon, and stray light has been shown to throw off that synchrony. What looks to us like a streetlight left on is, to a large fraction of the biosphere, a sustained and pointless shout.

We lived in the dark ourselves, and not just under it. The historian Roger Ekirch, combing diaries, medical texts, and court records, documented that preindustrial Europeans commonly slept in two shifts. They went to bed a couple of hours after dusk, slept deeply, then woke for an hour or so — a calm, unremarkable interval the records call the watch, occurring between the "first sleep" and the "second sleep." People prayed, reflected on dreams, read by rushlight, talked, tended the fire, visited neighbors, made love. Then they slept again until dawn. Nobody in those documents seems to have found any of this odd. The night apparently contained a room that we have since walled off.

The room may still be in the floor plan. In a small, famous experiment in the early 1990s, the researcher Thomas Wehr gave volunteers fourteen hours of darkness every day for weeks — no lamps, no screens, just the light a winter day provides. Their sleep gradually reorganized itself into the old pattern: two sleeps, with a quiet, lucid hour between, during which certain hormone levels rose. The pattern had been waiting in them the whole time, like a language learned in childhood. Electric light didn't merely extend the day. It may have amputated an intermission the rest of us didn't know we were missing.

The body keeps books on this. Around the turn of this century, researchers discovered a third kind of photoreceptor in the human retina — not rods, not cones, but cells whose job is simply to report brightness to the brain's master clock. They are tuned especially to blue light, which is why the white LEDs in our phones and kitchens are so biologically loud in the evening, and why dimming the screen helps more than dimming the room used to. Disrupt that signal long enough and the costs compound: disturbed sleep, metabolic problems, suppressed melatonin. Night shift work — the deliberate, industrial occupation of the hours the body expects to be dark — is classified by international health authorities as a probable human carcinogen. That's a startling sentence to write about a lighting choice, but the evidence has accumulated in the same direction for decades: the dark is not a luxury the body can do without.

In fairness, the lit night built its own world, and it's a world worth defending. The baker who starts at four so the bread exists by seven; the nurse on nights; the last bus and the first train; the diner at three in the morning where the strange and the sleepless keep their own society. There is a real country called Night that electric light opened for settlement — a place where the usual daytime distances between strangers drop, where the conversations happen that can't happen at noon. We kept that country. What we paved over was the other one: the biological night of two sleeps and a watch, the sky of a hundred thousand years. It didn't have to be either/or, but nobody was counting.

And the darkest thing you can see is also the deepest. On a decent night, away from cities, you can make out the Andromeda Galaxy without any equipment — a faint oval smudge, the farthest thing visible to the naked human eye, about two and a half million light-years away. Sit with that for a second. The photons striking your retina left Andromeda before our genus existed. When you look up at a truly dark sky, you are not looking at a ceiling; you are looking down a well of time, each layer of it a different age, the whole history of the universe stacked by distance and delivered to your eye for free. Every human who ever lived, until very recently, received this transmission nightly. It was the one shared context of the species — calendar, compass, clock, and scripture all at once.

That's what's being lost, and the numbers tell you the scale of it. In 2016, an international team published the first world atlas of artificial night sky brightness. More than eighty percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies. The Milky Way is hidden from roughly a third of all people alive — about sixty percent of Europeans and nearly eighty percent of North Americans — meaning that most citizens of wealthy countries have never seen the galaxy that contains their home. It is getting worse quickly. Depending on how you measure — citizen scientists with their eyes, or satellites from orbit — the night sky has been brightening by somewhere between two and ten percent every year. Compound a ten percent annual loss and within a human lifetime you arrive somewhere very close to total.

What evaporates isn't only prettiness. It's calibration — the felt, bodily sense of where we are: a lit island, adrift in something enormous. You can be told the universe is vast; that's information. Standing under a sky where the galaxy runs wall to wall is knowledge of a different kind, the kind that arrived in you before you had words for it, and it shaped everything: our myths, our clocks, our sense of scale and consequence. A civilization that loses the night sky doesn't just lose a view. It loses its most ancient instrument for feeling small in a way that was, oddly, mostly comforting. The stars were the original argument that the world is bigger than your problems, an argument delivered nightly and free of charge.

Meanwhile, a whole catalog of phenomena exists only on the far side of darkness, invisible the moment the lights come on. The zodiacal light — a faint pyramid of glow above the horizon after dusk, sunlight scattered off dust between the planets — shows only in pristine skies. The gegenschein, a dim patch directly opposite the sun, is fainter still. Auroras need dark to burn. Bioluminescent bays, where every stirred paddle stroke detonates into blue fire, wash out to nothing under a bright moon. Fireflies. Faint stars, findable only by not looking directly at them. Darkness, it turns out, is not the opposite of seeing. It is the other instrument, tuned to a whole register of reality that constant illumination renders permanently mute.

And attention, I suspect, works the same way. Under lights that never go off, everything flattens to the same brightness — every hour interchangeable, every surface lit to the same consumer-grade urgency. Some things are like faint stars: you meet them by looking slightly beside them, in the unplanned hour, in rest, in the interval we've engineered out of the night. I don't want to lean too hard on the metaphor. But it seems worth noticing that a permanently backlit life loses depth for roughly the same reason a city sky does.

The good news is that the repairs are cheap, boring, and already proven. Light that is pointed down instead of up. Light that is warm instead of blue-white. Light that is on only when someone is actually there — timers, motion sensors, shielded fixtures. Flagstaff, Arizona adopted dark-sky-friendly lighting decades ago and became the first certified Dark Sky City; Natural Bridges National Monument was the first Dark Sky Park, and the list now runs to hundreds. Turtles hatch and find the sea again on beaches that switched to amber. You don't have to move to a desert to get a piece of this back. You have to find one dark hour, now and then, and give your eyes the sixty minutes of work they were built to do — and then stand somewhere with your head tilted back, being reintroduced to your address.

When the power came back that night, decades ago now, it did so without ceremony. The streetlight at the corner snapped on, the refrigerator resumed its hum, and the Milky Way went out between one of my blinks and the next. But I had seen it, and seeing it is not reversible. That was the discovery the blackout handed me: the dark was never empty. It was full — of stars, of turtles and fireflies and sleeping birds, of the old second sleep, of light two and a half million years old falling out of the past onto an eight-year-old's face on a lawn in the suburbs. It was full, and we had simply stopped standing still, in the right kind of nothing, long enough to notice.
