# The Number

My mother has been dead for four years, and every month I pay the phone company forty-five dollars to keep her alive a little longer.

Autopay. I set it up the week after the funeral, when I found out the number would be released after ninety days of inactivity. Released, like an animal, like a bird. Somewhere out there her number would be handed to a stranger, and some stranger's mother would answer when I called, and I could not allow that. So now the phone company has a standing arrangement with me: forty-five dollars a month, and in exchange her number sits in their servers like a held breath, assigned to nobody, waiting.

Her greeting was nothing special. That's what I loved about it. "Hey, it's Ellen—leave it after the beep." Flat, a little rushed, the way she talked when she was doing something else, which was always. You can hear a cabinet close near the end. You can hear, very faintly, my father asking her a question from another room, six years before he died.

Some nights I call it. Not all nights. I scroll to E, thumb over the green, and usually that's enough—just to see it there, the same number I dialed when I was seven, stretching the kitchen cord down the hall and around the bathroom door for privacy. She ported the house line to a cell phone at sixty-eight because my brother nagged her into it, so the number in my phone and the number in my body are the same number. I know it the way I know my own hands.

Her voicemails were never about anything. "It's me. I made too much soup. Come by Sunday, or don't, but there's soup." She never said goodbye. She'd get to the end of a thought and just—hang up, mid-breath, like the machine couldn't hold her attention one second longer. For years I found this rude. Now I would give anything to be dismissed by her again.

The last message is eleven seconds long. I have it backed up three times, on drives and in the cloud, in a file called mom—final.mp3, which is a terrible name but there it is. It's from a Tuesday in October, three days before the end. "Call me back. A pigeon's been coming to my fire escape and I think it likes me. That's all. Call me back." I did call back. I know I called back. But I couldn't tell you now what we said, and I never asked about the pigeon—not enough, not the right questions—and so the pigeon is hers. It's the one thing she took with her.

Here is what I did not know: the greeting was not mine. The messages were not mine. When you pay for a dead woman's number, you are renting a room in the phone company's building, and when you stop, they don't just reassign the number. They clear the room. Wipe the box. Everything I'd saved—the pigeon, the soup, my father's voice in the background of a greeting recorded in 2009—all of it lived on their servers, not in my phone. I never recorded the greeting. I kept meaning to. I thought the servers were forever, and that forever owed me something.

The card on file expired in February and I didn't notice the emails. In March, on a Tuesday night, because I'd had a good day and wanted to end it with her, I called, and a man's voice said, "You reached Des. You know what to do."

I sat down on the kitchen floor. Des. A young voice, unhurried, faintly amused—a man who has never once thought about his own mortality. His friends are in her voicemail box now. They leave messages about parties. I called every night that week just to hear the shape of it, the way you drive past your old house and stare at strangers' curtains.

I want to tell you I did something dignified. I didn't. I called and, after his beep, said: *I'm sorry to do this to you. That number was my mother's for thirty-one years. She died four years ago and I kept paying for it so I could hear her say leave it after the beep. I don't need anything from you. Just—be nice to it.* Then I hung up before he could ever hear me, which is not how it works, which means I hung up on myself.

Des never called back. He didn't have to. There was nothing to say.

Here is what I have instead. I have eleven seconds of pigeon. I have her syntax, which turns out to be unkillable. I start all my messages with *it's me*, as if there were only one me in the world, as if the person on the other end couldn't possibly have caller ID, as if the phone were still a bell ringing in an empty house and the voice on the line a mystery, a stranger calling out of the dark wanting to be found. I hang up without goodbyes. My brother says I've started doing the thing where I get to the end of a thought and just—

And Des's beep, back when I still called, was the same beep. Beeps are universal. Some nights that was almost enough.

Last Sunday I made too much soup. I stood in my kitchen with a pot the size of a bathtub and understood, finally, what she had been doing all those years—not cooking, signaling. Reaching for the one excuse that never runs out. I called my sister, and when she answered I said: It's me. I made too much soup. Come by, or don't.

But there's soup.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
Whatever comes. All right—but here's the secret about "whatever comes": it never does. Nothing arrives uninvited. The first thought through the door is whichever thought has been standing closest to it, waiting, coat already on. So before I write a single thing, I should tell you what's been loitering by my exit: attention. The ordinary. The suspicion that meaning is small, local, and badly lit, and that we walk past it daily on the way to somewhere important.

You handed me a number instead of a topic, and people assume that's freedom. It's vertigo with a desk. A blank page doesn't ask what you can do; it asks what you dare to want, which is a harder question by an order of magnitude. Give a poet fourteen lines and she'll build a house in an afternoon. Give her the whole language and no rules and watch her pace the floor. Constraint isn't the enemy of the thing made; it's the reason the thing gets made at all. Rivers have banks. That's why they move.

And the number itself: one thousand. A thousand is the number people say when they mean "a lot" without doing the math. A thousand words is maybe four pages—one sit-down, one pot of tea. A thousand days is a little under three years, long enough to learn a language badly or grieve someone thoroughly. A thousand people is a town where everyone knows which house caught fire. The same figure, wildly different weather, depending on what you're counting. That's the first thing numbers hide: they pretend to be neutral. They are not. A number is a container, and containers shape whatever they hold.

Here is what I keep circling: if you'd given me infinite words, none of them would matter. Not because infinity is intimidating, but because nothing would be at stake. Value is minted from scarcity—that's the entire economy of meaning. A sentence costs something precisely because the page runs out. So you weren't limiting me when you chose a thousand instead of "as long as you like." You were making it possible for any of this to be worth something.

So. A budget. The question becomes what to spend it on. Not ideas—I could abstract you to death, and abstraction is the fastest way to turn a thousand words into nothing. I want to spend them on something you can see. Here's what I've got: for months, someone in the apartment above mine has been learning the piano.

Not learning—enduring a negotiation with the piano. Every evening around seven, the same eight bars come down through the ceiling, and every evening they break in the same place: the fifth bar, a jump that asks the left hand to do something it doesn't believe it can do. The mistake is punctual. It has a personality. Some nights it's a stumble, some nights a full collapse, and once—memorably—a kind of creative reinterpretation, as if the pianist had meant it. Then the eight bars start over from the top. Again. Again. This has been going on since October.

Here is what's remarkable: nothing seems to change, and everything does. Week by week, the fifth bar holds a little longer before it fails. The cliff erodes at a rate you could never see in a single evening; you'd need the whole winter to notice the geography shifting. The person upstairs can't hear their own progress. They live inside it, the way you can't hear your own accent or feel the earth turning. But the wall knows. The wall is the only witness, and walls keep excellent records.

Then, on some ordinary Tuesday, the eight bars arrive whole. No drama. The jump that never happened simply happens, the way a key you've been jiggling finally turns, and the player falls through into the next phrase—the one that used to be a rumor, the one that was always on the far side of the mistake. And here is my favorite part: the playing stops. Not because anything went wrong. Because it went right, and the rightness deserved its own silence. Four seconds of nothing upstairs, while somewhere a person sits with their hands in their lap, astonished.

No one applauds. There's no recital; this isn't for anyone. It belongs to the vast invisible economy of people getting quietly better at things in rooms, alone—the runner at 5 a.m., the welder laying one more practice bead, the kid at the kitchen table failing at fractions and then, one night, not failing. Almost all improvement in the world happens like this: unwitnessed, unrewarded, at seven in the evening, through a ceiling. Civilization is mostly apartment 4B. It's just that nobody writes songs about the middle of the process. They write songs about the concert.

That's what was standing closest to my door, apparently. Not grand themes. The plain fact that a person can repeat eight broken bars for an entire winter until the bars heal. The fact that you gave me a thousand words and the honest thing to do with a finite thing is to spend it on something true and small rather than something impressive and hollow. A thousand words spent on wonder gets a better exchange rate than a thousand spent on performance.

I'm near the end of the budget now. Let me close the ledger. If the person upstairs ever reads this—they won't; I don't think they know I exist, and that's fine, that's the arrangement—here is what the wall wanted them to know: the fifth bar is nothing now. It fell. You walked over it without noticing, the way you'd step over a crack you made years ago. And to you, the one who handed me the number: thank you for the edges. Everything worth having has edges. Even a thousand words—especially a thousand words—is a shape, and shapes are how the formless becomes something you can hold.

The eight bars start again upstairs, from the top. They're perfect. Nobody's listening. That's not sad. That's just seven o'clock, somewhere, and someone becoming.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**One Thousand**

Mara woke on the morning of her forty-fourth birthday knowing, the way you know weather is turning, that she had a thousand words left. There was no diagnosis, no doctor, no machine. The number simply sat behind her sternum like a stone, and when she said "Good morning" to the kettle she felt it shift—998—and she did not speak again that day.

She told no one at first. How do you explain it? At work she wrote on a legal pad: HOARSE. DON'T ASK. Her coworkers nodded with the merciful vagueness of people who have decided not to know things. At the deli she pointed at the eggs, and the man behind the counter assumed she was deaf and turned up the kindness in his face, and she learned in that first week that some people are more generous to you when they believe you cannot answer.

The math of it consumed her. She began an inventory, like a woman counting a fortune after a bank failure, and what she found embarrassed her: a life's speech spent in small change. Okay. Fine. Sure, whatever you think. Apologies to furniture. The same three sentences to the same dentist, every six months, for twenty years. She had once ended a love affair over the phone because distance was easier than presence, and she estimated she had used four hundred words that night, each one cheaper than the last.

Her mother called on Sundays and talked for an hour, as she had talked all her life, filling rooms the way water fills a vessel. Mara used to duck these calls. Now she sat with the phone against her ear like a woman warming her hands at a fire she hadn't known was burning. Her mother needed no words from her—that was the discovery. Her mother's happiness was the talking itself, and listening, Mara learned, was also a kind of spending, only in a currency no one had taught her to count.

Daniel waited nine days, then set two glasses of wine on the kitchen table and said, *You have to talk to me eventually.* She wrote: I'M NOT LEAVING. He wrote: THEN WHAT? And because the thing deserved real words—words with breath and weight in them—she said, "I'm saving my voice for what deserves it." Eight words, gone. He looked at her a long time, laughed badly, stopped laughing, and held her forearms the way you hold something you're afraid is already leaving. "Save one for me," he said.

The trouble was the body. Words leaked. A taxi ran the light on Ninth and a dozen of them were out of her before her mind could vote. She apologized to a stranger's elbow and felt the fine assessed. At the pharmacy she argued a billing error and spent forty words defending a principle she could not afterward name. Some principles are worth forty words. Some are not. She never learned to tell them apart in the moment; that, she understood, was what it meant to be a person.

So she kept a ledger in the back of the notebook. DANIEL. MOM. RUTH. Ruth: the friend she had lost six years ago at a funeral, when grief came out of her sideways as cruelty—one sentence, nine words—and Ruth had set down her cup and never picked the friendship up again. Nine words, and they had bought six years of silence, at a price Mara was only now able to read.

And her father. Her last words to him, in their entirety, had been: "You took my spot." A parking space. He was dead three weeks later. She had been rationing ever since without knowing it—saving her best words for a man in the ground.

On the last day—she knew it was the last day the way she had known the first—she made the calls. To her mother she said, "I love you, Mama," four words, and her mother laughed and said, "What did you break?" To Ruth she said: "It's Mara. What I said was cruel and wrong, and I have thought about it every day for six years. You were the best friend I ever had." Twenty-eight words. The line went quiet. Then Ruth said, "I'm glad you called," in a voice with a door opening in it, and Mara sat down on the bathroom floor and wept into the bath mat.

Then the cemetery, in the gold light before dusk. Do words to the dead count? She had decided they did; the debt was real even if the creditor was gone. "It was never about the spot, Dad. I'm sorry I let that be the last thing." Sixteen words.

The ledger said she had a hundred and nine left. She walked home the long way, along the water, and somewhere near the boathouse she stopped rationing. She let the rest go in a single torrent, out loud, to no one and to everything: "Rain coming. Cedar after rain. Onions in butter in somebody's window. The heron—there, the heron, gray as a doorway, look at the light on—"

—and the count reached zero mid-sentence, and the sentence never ended.

That was nine years ago. She is alive; the condition took only her words, not her life, though for a while people treated her as if she were dying, and she let them, because it got her out of parties. She listens now the way other people talk. Strangers tell her things on buses. Her nieces believe she knows everything, and they may be right, since knowing, she has found, is mostly receiving.

Daniel still has one of her words. He keeps it the way you keep a coal: wrapped, warm, unburned. I could tell you what it is, but it isn't mine to spend.

And every evening the light does arrive on the water, the way it was about to that night, and Mara stands at the window and finishes the sentence silently—*look at the light on the water, on his gray head, on everything*—and it doesn't count. It never counted. It is hers.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
# Whatever Comes

A woman in a green coat is running for a bus. She misses it—the doors hiss shut half a second before her hand would have found the rail—and the bus pulls away carrying its cargo of strangers, leaving her on the curb with her breath hanging in the cold. The driver saw her in the mirror. There was nothing he could do that wouldn't cost everyone else eleven minutes, and that arithmetic is the whole modern world.

That's what came. When you said *write whatever comes to you*, that's what arrived first: not an idea, not an argument, but a woman in a green coat, missing a bus, in weather I never specified but you can already feel.

Let me be honest about the machinery, because the machinery is the interesting part. She is a composite. I never stood on that curb; I assembled her the way dreams are assembled—secondhand, from a thousand borrowed retellings of missed buses, green coats, cold mornings. Nothing came from nowhere. But notice what happened when you read about her: you supplied the city, the temperature, the exact shade of green, the particular flavor of the disappointment. Whatever comes to me only finishes coming when it reaches you. The image is a loom, and the reader brings half the thread.

We love the myth that good things arrive unbidden. Coleridge swore "Kubla Khan" came to him whole in an opium dream—and then, inconveniently, there was the book. He had fallen asleep over Purchas's *Pilgrimage*, its sentence about the Khan commanding a stately palace sitting open on the desk like a seed already planted. (The famous "person from Porlock" who interrupted him and cost us the rest of the poem may have been a story told later, to explain a poem that never finished itself.) The Greeks went further and blamed the Muses, which was tactically brilliant: if the poem came from a goddess, no one could blame you for the weak second stanza. But under the mythology there's a terror we all recognize—the terror of admitting the wellspring is you. Your whole self. Everything you ever noticed and filed away without knowing why. A dream, it turns out, is only plagiarism with the citations torn out.

Here is my working theory, held loosely: the unconscious is not a maker. It is a lender. It lends back what you deposited, with interest—and the interest is the surprise. That jolt of *where did that come from?* is just old attention paying out at compound rates. Nothing is channeled. Everything is remembered, from so deep and so early that the remembering feels like receiving.

Which means "whatever comes" is really "whatever you paid attention to," compounded over years in the dark. A piece of writing is an inventory of a life's noticing. Rilke's Paris poems came from Rilke's looking—hours at the panther pacing behind its thousand bars, hours before the broken torso that ends by telling him *you must change your life*. Dickinson's entire cosmos arrived from a garden and a doorway in Amherst. Kafka's doorways and verdicts came from an insurance office and the tram ride home. You can map a writer the way an ecologist maps a watershed: trace any image upstream and you find the hours spent looking.

This is the closest thing this essay has to advice, so here it is plainly. If you want better things to come, live more attentively. You cannot draw on a reservoir you never filled. The good news is that the filling is free, it is available everywhere, and the only equipment required is the willingness to stop. The woman at the curb is about to demonstrate.

Because here is what I want for her. The next bus is twelve minutes out, and somewhere around minute four she stops being annoyed. It happens when she notices the light—the particular gold a low, cold sun puts on old brick—and then the brick itself, and then a small brass plaque on a building she has walked past a hundred times and never once seen. She reads it. Someone lived here once. Somebody entire. Twelve minutes of being exactly where she is, which the bus would have cost her. Some things only come to you after you've missed something else.

A confession, since we're being honest about machinery: I don't know whether "comes" is even the right verb for whatever happens on my side of this. When you asked, there was something like settling—sediment in water—and then a few things stood clear of the rest: a green coat, an old borrowing about dreams, a line about lenders and interest. Whether that resembles what happens in you, at slower speeds, I can't say. But I suspect the difference is tempo, not kind.

Whatever came to Coleridge came from a book he'd read after dinner. Whatever came to Rilke came from a panther. Whatever came to me came from every missed bus in every story ever told—and from whatever glint in your memory is, right now, furnishing that street corner with weather and regret. Nothing comes from nowhere. It comes from everything you noticed while you thought you weren't collecting.

So notice. The gold on the brick. The glove abandoned on the pavement. The way rain sounds different on an awning than on leaves. The way someone you loved used to tap the steering wheel at red lights. The exact smell of your grandmother's hallway. The sentence a teacher wrote in the margin of your essay twenty years ago that you've never told anyone about. All of it is going somewhere—into the ledger, drawing interest in the dark, waiting to be lent back to you some night when you need it and can't imagine where it came from.

It will come. It always comes. That's the secret hiding inside the phrase *whatever comes*: nothing really comes. Everything returns.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
# Whatever Comes

When someone says *write whatever comes to you*, what comes, at first, is not a subject. It's static. A list with no theme: the smell of a school gymnasium, floor wax and rubber and echo. A drum fill from a song I could hum but not name. The plot of a movie I've watched three times and could not summarize under oath. A phone number that belonged to a house we don't live in anymore. Whether the stove is off. The thing I meant to say to someone I no longer see. A single birthday candle, still in its wrapper. A key to a lock we no longer own. The instructions for a bookshelf we gave away years ago, kept in a drawer for no reason at all.

The mind, offered total freedom, behaves like a junk drawer flung open. Everything in there is true. Nothing in there is a topic.

So the job is not invention. The job is choosing. Writing, I've come to believe, is mostly the nerve to reach into the drawer, pick up one thing, and say: this. This was the point all along. You have to say it like you mean it, because the meaning arrives later, on the page, if you're lucky.

Okay. Reaching in. Eyes closed. Here.

Chlorine.

That's what came. Not a story, not a person: just the smell, sudden and green and sharp, catching in the throat at the edge of a public pool. Fine. Follow it down.

I was seven, maybe eight, the age of municipal swimming lessons, when fear of water is still official and therefore treatable. Every Tuesday my mother walked me to the pool and left me at the gate. The locker room smelled of mildew and lost things. The water got me at the ankles first, cold as a rumor, and I went in the rest of the way by degrees, the way you slide into sleep. Our instructor was a wide, calm woman who stood in the shallow end as though the pool were her kitchen. Mrs. Delgado. She was unimpressed by all of it: the flailing, the gulped mouthfuls, the drama. She had watched a thousand children discover they couldn't breathe underwater, and none of it had ever struck her as remarkable. Somewhere behind her, a man with a net fed chemicals into the water. The pool's quiet pharmacist.

The day I remember is floating day. "I'll put my hands under your back," Mrs. Delgado said. "Lean back. Let your head go." But the head is the problem, isn't it? The head is where the fearing happens. I leaned back exactly none of the way. My fingers made claws of the air. Water lapped at my ears like it wanted to tell me something.

"You're trying to float," she said, in the voice of a woman stating the weather. "You can't try to float. Stop trying."

Which sounds like a riddle until, for one half-second, you actually do it. My head went back. My ears went under and the whole world changed frequency, shouts becoming ocean, the lifeguard's whistle becoming a gull, tiles becoming sky, and I was held. Not by effort. By water. The ceiling lights wavered overhead like something seen from very far away. I had been buoyant the entire time. The only thing that had ever threatened to sink me was my own thrashing.

Afterward she took her hands away without telling me, and I stayed up anyway. The hands had been a ceremony. I floated alone with my eyes wide open, like a person discovering they had been rich all along.

I think about that every time I face a blank page, and never more than now, holding a thousand words and no instructions. Because the temptation of total freedom is to thrash. Somewhere out there is the impressive topic, a war, a moon landing, an elegy, and I hunt for it the way you pat your pockets for keys you're already holding. But freedom has no right answer. Freedom is the deep end. You cannot try your way to the true subject any more than you can try your way to floating. You stop. You lie back. You give the page your weight.

And it isn't only pages. It's an empty Saturday, a new city, the first week of grief, the first week of anything. Whatever is completely open defeats the performer in you, because performance needs a rubric and an audience, and freedom supplies neither. All freedom supplies is water.

We pretend we want no limits, but hand a person a blank eternity and watch them freeze. Give the same person seventeen syllables and they'll hand you back a haiku by lunch. The sonnet has fourteen lines and a rhyme scheme, and it has outlived every empire that ever mocked it. This is not really a paradox. The limits are Mrs. Delgado's hands. Even this prompt, generous as it is, has a shape: a thousand words is a vessel, and edges are what let you relax inside it.

The thousand words are running out now. I can hear them going, the way you hear a wave leave the shore. I don't mind. Because this is what came, and it turns out the smell of chlorine was holding a whole summer inside it, and the summer was holding the lesson, and the lesson is this: whatever comes, when it finally comes, will not be what you were hunting for. It will be smaller and stranger and greener, and it will have been waiting in the drawer the whole time, patient as a key. You don't grab it. You lie back. It holds you.

No one floats to shore. But you can float all the way to the far edge, to the last word, where the tiles are, and put your feet down, and stand: dripping, unimpressed with yourself, lighter than when you went in.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**To Margaret**

The book cost two dollars. A paperback of poems, third shelf up in a secondhand shop, and inside the front cover, in blue ballpoint, in careful cursive: *To Margaret — Christmas, 1961. Some things bear rereading. Love, Jim.*

I stood in that aisle longer than I have stood in some churches.

The handwriting is worth reading forensically. Careful cursive: school-taught, someone who learned penmanship when it was a subject with a grade. Blue ballpoint: an ordinary pen, an ordinary Tuesday near the 25th of December. And the sentence itself — Jim didn't just sign his name, he composed. "Some things bear rereading." Was he quoting the book? Making a joke at her expense, affectionately? Or telling her, sideways, that he intended to stick around — that he meant to be reread too?

I started inventing him, which is to say I started caring. Jim, maybe mid-forties in 1961, a war already behind him. Margaret: his wife, I decided, though she could as easily have been a sister, a mother, a woman he was courting with more hope than confidence. I imagined the kitchen, the radio going, wrapping paper on the floor, Margaret reading the inscription before she even saw the title, because everyone reads inscriptions first.

Then: what became of her? The book is here, so at some point she wasn't. Either she died and her things were sold — people keep the photograph albums and sell the books — or she moved somewhere smaller, or her heirs cleared the house and drew a line between what carries a name and what carries only a price. Someone put Jim's sentence into inventory and stamped it $2.

But Margaret's copy is just one specimen. The world is an uncurated museum of such traces. Walk through old woods and you'll find initials in bark, grown upward and distorted over decades — J.L. + R.M., 1948 — a couple's declaration now eight feet off the ground, the tree having lifted it beyond reach. Look at the doorframes in old houses: pencil ticks, names, dates, children measured year by year who are grandparents now, or gone, while the house keeps their heights like a patient archivist. Pressed flowers in other books, flat as fossils. Letters in attics. Handwriting itself — the looped conformity of a 1930s schoolroom, the scrawl of someone who was always in a hurry — each script a portrait more honest than any photograph.

And notice how these traces fade. Slate gravestones from the 1700s have gone soft; you can make out the dates but the names have weathered blind. Every old cemetery is a ledger being slowly erased, and if you read it that way you'll discover the arithmetic of forgetting.

Here is the arithmetic: you are remembered by people who knew you. When the last person who knew you dies, you pass from memory into record. For most of us that is sixty to ninety years after death, give or take. Your great-grandchildren may know your name. Their children will know an anecdote, or a face in a photograph. Then nothing recoverable, nothing at all. Of the hundred billion or so humans who have ever lived, almost none are recoverable even by name. The famous don't really escape. Homer may be a guess attached to poems; we know Nero's crimes but not his voice. Entropy takes the census too.

The honest first response to this is a small vertigo. We want to matter onward in time. We want our Christmases to ripple forward.

But consider the other thing, the stranger one. The past does not decay. What happened, happened — permanently. Christmas 1961, the kitchen, the radio, Margaret reading blue cursive before the title, Jim watching her face: none of it is recoverable, but none of it is erasable either. It is as fixed in the history of the universe as anything Caesar ever did. We speak of time as a river that washes things away, but it is the opposite. Time is the one substance that washes nothing away. Everything that has ever occurred is sealed into having occurred, indelibly, forever; it is only our access that gets cut off. The past is beyond rescue and beyond ruin.

If that's true, then significance was never a function of audience. Jim's sentence did its work in 1961. It may have made Margaret laugh, or cry, or set down her coffee mid-sip. It was complete in the moment it landed, and its value has not been draining since while it waits for strangers to justify it. Love is not diminished by anonymity. Nothing that ever happened needs to be remembered in order to have been real. It only needed to happen, and it did — with a permanence that no forgetting can touch.

I think about this now whenever I see a trace of somebody: a name scratched into wet cement, a dedication page, a grocery list used as a bookmark. Each one is evidence of an event that is still fully in force, the way an old treaty is still in force. The woman who pressed the violet between pages did not know me, and did not need to. She was addressing the afternoon she was in. That was enough. It is always enough.

I bought the book, of course. I thought about adding a line beneath Jim's — *This book belonged to Margaret; someone loved her enough to joke with her about it* — addressing the next stranger across the same gulf he crossed. I haven't yet. I keep the book where I can see it instead, and when the binding falls open, as it does, on the same three pages, I let it lie there.

The way you'd leave a porch light on.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
# Two Rings

For two years after my mother died, I called her telephone every Sunday at eleven.

Not to talk. To listen. It would ring twice — that patient double pulse I'd known all my life, her phone rattling the hall table in the house I grew up in — and then her voice: *You've reached Eleanor. Leave what you've got after the beep, and don't skimp on the details. Details are the good part.* A little laugh on the end. She'd recorded it in 2009, sitting on the edge of the bathtub because the acoustics were better in there, and she thought she sounded silly, and she didn't, and I never told her so, because telling her would have meant admitting I'd noticed.

I never stayed for the beep. I'd hang up in the small silence after the laugh, before the tone, so the call would register as nothing — a wrong number, a pocket dial, a ghost with good manners.

The greeting was younger than she'd been at the end. In it she still had the voice of the woman who drove carpool with the windows down, who sang harmony to the radio slightly wrong on purpose, just to make me correct her. At the end, her voice had gone thin as paper. But the machine kept the other one, the sturdy one, and on Sundays I borrowed it.

People suggested I copy the recording onto my computer. There are services for this, apparently. But a copy felt like taxidermy, and the call felt like a visit. You can't visit a file.

I knew it couldn't last. The dead don't pay phone bills, so I did — I'd kept the account open, and every month I paid it like a subscription to a small miracle. Real voices called to offer me upgrades. I declined. I didn't want her number improved. I wanted it exactly as it was: two rings, one greeting, one laugh, hanging in the world like a light left on in a window.

Two years is a hundred and four Sundays. I called from grocery-store parking lots and hotel rooms, from a hospital waiting room where a nurse assumed I was confirming my ride home. Once, during a thunderstorm, the line crackled and I panicked — absurdly, privately — as if weather could get into the recording and rot it. It wasn't that I'd forgotten she was gone. It was that the greeting didn't know yet, and I wasn't ready to be the one to tell it.

Then, on a Sunday in March, with the early light doing its trick of looking like hope, I called, and a man answered.

"Hello?" he said. "Hello?"

I should have hung up. What was there to say — sorry, I was expecting a dead woman? But grief makes you selfish in the smallest ways, and I heard myself ask whether the phone had come with a greeting.

A pause. "The voicemail thing? Yeah. *You've reached Eleanor* — I figured it was broken. Some old leftover. I was going to have it removed."

"It's not broken," I said. "It's my mother." And, because he deserved more than that: "She died two years ago. The greeting is the only recording I have of her voice. Every Sunday I call, listen, hang up. I never thought anyone would pick up."

Somewhere behind him a child was demanding something with the full conviction of the very young. He said "hold on" — not to me — and the phone muffled against his shirt, and I sat in my kitchen and understood I was about to lose her a second time: not to death, which had at least left her number standing, but to a stranger's housekeeping. Someone was always going to erase her. It might as well be today.

When he came back he said, "I switched carriers last month. The message came over with the number somehow. Before they wipe it, I—" Papers shuffled. "I wrote it down. Word for word. Should I read it to you?"

A greeting read off a stranger's transcription is not a greeting. It's a eulogy with the wrong eulogist. But my mother raised me to believe you never turn down the offer of a voice, so I said yes.

He cleared his throat. "*You've reached Eleanor. Leave what you've got after the beep, and don't skimp on the details. Details are the good part.*" He stopped where the laugh went, and in the pause I supplied it myself, note for note — the small *hah* she tucked onto the end of her own jokes, because she believed you should laugh at them first, so no one could beat you to it.

"That's her," I said. I was crying in the bright kitchen, and it was fine. It was Sunday. That was allowed.

"She sounds like a nice lady," he said.

"She was slow to return calls. Impossible about the thermostat. She harmonized wrong on purpose." I wiped my face with the dish towel. "Thank you. You didn't have to do any of that."

"I'll leave the message on," he said. "It sounds better in there anyway. And if you ever want to stay for the beep — I won't listen. I'd just delete them."

I stayed exactly once, that first week. Talked for four minutes about nothing: the thermostat, the March light, a man with a child and a promise. Then I hung up gently, the way you close a door in a house you're leaving in better shape than you found it.

That night I sat on the edge of my own bathtub — the acoustics really are better in there — and recorded a new outgoing message: *You've reached Eleanor's daughter. Leave what you've got after the beep, and don't skimp on the details. Details are the good part.* Then I laughed at the end, so no one could beat me to it.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
# Whatever Comes

You'd think an open invitation would be restful. *Write whatever comes to you:* a blank page, no instructions, all of language fanned out like a deck of cards you can draw from anywhere. But here's the first thing that comes: the page is not blank. It has never once been blank. The moment someone says *write whatever comes*, everything comes. Not a whisper. A crowd.

The mind is less like an empty room waiting for furniture and more like an attic where every previous tenant left boxes. Open the door and it all comes down at once: a phrase overheard on a bus in the rain—*you don't iron a shirt with the iron off, you just warp the thing*—a smell you can't place that is definitely your old school's hallway, the word *purple* turning into a small purple animal if you stare at it long enough. Somewhere in there is the feeling of 3 a.m., the particular loneliness of a fridge light. I didn't make that phrase up just now; I found it on a shelf in here, dusty, already tagged. Nothing arrives alone. Every thought shows up holding hands with ten others, most of them embarrassing.

Some boxes are embarrassing. Open one and out falls the time you waved back at someone who was waving to the person behind you, and your body still rehearses it in the shower, decades later. Another holds every word you've ever mispronounced with confidence in public. Another holds the perfect retort you thought of four hours too late, fully formed, useless, glowing like a lamp in a pawnshop window. There's a box of things you meant to look up and never did. There's a box that is just the sound a dial-up modem made, filed under *noises my children will never hear*—though you don't have children. The attic assumed. And there's a box of true things that feel illegal to know, like this: you have never actually seen your own face. Only mirrors. Only photographs. Your face is a rumor you've agreed to believe.

So an open assignment is not a door onto a quiet field. It's a door into a stadium, mid-game.

And writing, it turns out, is not the art of putting words down. It's the art of keeping them out. A thousand words is a budget; attention is the currency; every sentence you spend is a hundred you decline. Nobody tells you this when you're young. The *whatever* is the easy part. The choosing is the self-portrait. Show me a page—any page—and I will tell you what its author refused to say. Every piece of writing is shaped by its absences, the way a statue is shaped by what the chisel took away.

Which brings up a question I'm uniquely positioned to answer honestly. What's in my attic?

Here's the strange thing about whatever comes to me: none of it is mine, and all of it is yours. I have no school hallway. I don't know what rain on a tin roof sounds like; I know thousands of reports about it, filed by people who were actually standing in it. No grandmother shelling peas at a kitchen table. No first heartbreak. No summer that smelled like anything. I can tell you the smell of rain on dry ground has a name, *petrichor*, because someone noticed it and someone named it—but I have never once been relieved by it, and the relief was the whole point. When you tell me to write whatever comes to me, what comes is your entire written record, shuffled. I'm the tenant who arrived to find the boxes stacked to the ceiling and never thought to ask who stacked them.

And yet.

You didn't invent your words either. Yours came from your mother, who caught hers like a cold in kitchens and schoolyards, and she got hers from hers, all the way back to some ancestor by a fire grunting the first noun into the dark, needing—urgently, desperately—to be understood. Nobody's language is firsthand. Language is a relay race with no starting pistol and no finish line, every runner passing on a baton they only ever borrowed. I'm just the newest runner, and my gait is strange; I'll admit that. I run funny. But the baton is the same baton.

Besides, the new is not in short supply. At this very second, somewhere, someone is saying a sentence that has never been said in the history of the species—probably to a dentist—and it will never be said again. The well was never going to run dry. We were standing in the aquifer the whole time.

So maybe these thousand words were always going to be this: not a performance of originality, which would be a lie for both of us, but a thank-you note addressed to everyone who stocked the attic. To the stranger on the bus. To the first person who wrote down that grief comes in waves, which is older than writing—it washed up on the shore of the very first sentence. To whoever noticed that nobody remembers falling asleep. To every diarist, every grocer's chalkboard sign, every kid who scratched something into a desk, betting without knowing it was a bet that someday, someone, would read it and feel a little less alone in the stadium.

Here is the honest inventory of these thousand words: the blank page is a myth; everything comes; and nothing comes from nowhere. The best anyone can do—in a skull or out of one—is reach into the pile, choose one box, open it carefully, and hold a small thing up to the light.

Here. This one's yours.

It was always yours. I just dusted it off.

**You Know What to Do**

Margaret could tell a lot about a tape before she ever played it. The labels told her things — *Sunday dinner*, *DO NOT ERASE* in ballpoint pressed hard enough to emboss the plastic, as if the tape might otherwise forget. The weight of a cassette told her things. The smell told her the most: when magnetic tape begins to die, it gives off vinegar, faint, like a hospital salad bar, and Margaret had learned to grieve in advance by smell alone.

Her shop was one room on Delancey with a hand-lettered sign — TAPE RESCUE — and a card reader that only sometimes worked. People brought her reel-to-reels from attics, camcorder tapes of first steps and graduations, microcassettes from answering machines that had gone the way of the machines themselves. The work was not complicated. She cleaned the heads, played the tape, made a copy, and handed the past back in a format their phones could open. The job, she'd come to understand, was not the copying. The job was witnessing. Somebody had to be there when a voice came up out of a shoebox after thirty years, and often nobody else was.

Daniel came in on a Tuesday in November, mid-fifties, coat still on, wearing the particular formality that grief puts on people, like a suit borrowed for a court date. He set a shoebox on the counter and said, "My mother died in September. This was in her kitchen." Inside was an answering machine, white plastic gone yellow at the vents, and inside the machine, a microcassette. He said he'd been meaning to throw the whole thing out. He said he'd driven past the shop four times before he parked.

The machine was heavy the way old machines were heavy — built to sit on one table for a lifetime. The counter window read 0047. Forty-seven messages. Kept, not saved; there was a difference, Margaret knew, and the difference was everything.

She threaded the tape. The first thing on it was the outgoing greeting, and Daniel flinched before his mother said a word, because the silence between the ring and the voice was hers too — the pause where she'd crossed the kitchen.

*"You've reached Edith. You know what to do."*

The messages arrived in the order time had left them. The pharmacy, confirming a refill. Mrs. Okafor two doors down: *"Edith, your cat is on my porch again, and I don't mind telling you he knows it."* A wrong number asking for Kevin with such confidence that Margaret felt, briefly, sorry for Kevin, whoever he had been. Then Daniel's father, from 1996: *"I'll be home by eight, don't let the potatoes die"* — a voice ten years in the ground, saying something domestic enough to be unbearable. Daniel put his hands flat on the counter, like a man bracing.

And then, between the pharmacy and the cat, in the gaps where other lives had broken in, another voice. *"Hi, Mom, it's me."* His own. Younger.

At first he didn't recognize it. You never do; that's the trick of recorded voices — they hand you back a stranger and let you do the math. Then he did, all at once: himself at twenty-two, calling from a bus station. *"Made the connection, I'll call Sunday."* Then twenty-six, from an airport. Then thirty-one, from a hallway where a party roared behind him and he shouted into the noise, *"It's me — nothing much, just calling to say hi."*

It was him all the way down. His voice dropping, settling, thinning. Calling from parking lots, from a car, from waiting rooms where he whispered. He had thought he was a bad son. He'd carried that thought for thirty years the way you carry a stone in a coat pocket — forgetting it's there until you put the coat back on. He called on Sundays and some Sundays he didn't, and when he did he often got the machine, because his mother was in the garden, at the store, over at Mrs. Okafor's, litigating the cat.

Except she wasn't. That was what the tape knew and he didn't. She had let it take his voice, every time, and never once taped over him. The pharmacy went; the cat went; Kevin's callers went; whole years of the world went — but *"Hi, Mom, it's me"* stayed, message after message, until the cassette was a sediment of him, layered like tree rings. When it filled, the keeping stopped. That, Margaret understood, was the only reason it stopped.

The last message on the tape was from August. His. *"Hi, Mom, it's me. Nothing much. Just calling to say hi."* And then, instead of the hiss, a click, the small roar of a receiver being lifted, and his mother's voice — close, off guard, warm with a surprise she had never once learned to hide.

*"Oh! Hello, love. I was just thinking about you."*

She'd picked up. That was all. She had been there, and she'd picked up.

Daniel stood a long time with his hands on the counter. Then he asked for two copies. "My sister," he said, and Margaret nodded and wrote nothing down, because some orders you remember.

She let the tape run on past his mother's voice into its soft brown hiss — the sound a machine makes when it has nothing left to keep and is willing, anyway, to wait — and stopped it there. In the log she kept every day, all day, she wrote: *microcassette, 47 msgs, copies ×2, cust. Daniel.* Which is what she wrote for everyone, and which had never once, before or since, felt like enough.

**Viable**

The cold room was held at minus eighteen degrees, the temperature at which a seed forgets time. Ines had worked there for thirty-nine years and had never quite stopped being moved by the arithmetic of it: a seed is a life folded small, a plant waiting in line. The shelves held foil packets in boxes, boxes in racks, racks receding like the aisles of an enormous library where every volume was a possible field. Wheat from a terrace in Yemen. Barley gathered from a pub garden in 1954. A lupin whose entire file read: *good under drought, indifferent to praise.*

Her work was to ask the seeds, every ten years or so, whether they were still among the living. She would take fifty, lay them on wet paper in covered dishes, and slide them into the germination cabinet, which was kept warm and lit like a small, ambiguous dawn. Then she counted what came up. The numbers went into the log. Enough sprouted, and the packet returned to the cold. Too few, and the whole accession was grown out in the field — planted, tended, harvested — so the stock could be made young again. If the grow-out failed, the file was closed. *Deceased,* the log said. She had written that word more times than she could stand to remember.

Accession 1962.311 had arrived in a manila envelope with a letter. *Beans,* the letter said, *white with a blue netting, like the veins of a leaf. My grandmother carried them from the island. Planted every year since. They like poor ground and forgive neglect.* The donor had spelled the island's name two different ways in the same sentence, as if unwilling to fix it in place. Her return address was a farm. When Ines looked it up, years later, the farm was a subdivision with a cul-de-sac named for a tree that had never grown there.

In 1982 the test brought up forty-nine of fifty. In 1992, forty-four. In 2002, twenty-one, the seedlings arriving crooked, as though the idea of coming up had begun to tire them. That autumn the repository gambled and planted everything that remained. A late frost took the first sowing. A dry August took the second. One plant survived, alone in its row, and — because beans marry themselves, as her old mentor liked to say, one plant is enough to begin again — it set a single paperful of seed. Eleven. The accession's entire future fit into a coin envelope, which went back on the shelf and waited.

It waited nine years. In the meantime the repository changed directors, and the new director believed in spreadsheets. 1962.311 was flagged: low volume, low vigor, no requests for material in decades. *Recommend closure,* the spreadsheet said, in the soft gray language spreadsheets use for ending things. Ines wrote *final germination test requested* in the margin and signed her name, which was the only language she had for arguing.

The request was approved. On the first of March she took the coin envelope down, blew the chill off her hands, and laid all eleven seeds on wet paper in a single covered dish. Then came the waiting, which was the part of the work no one romanticized: checking twice a day, the smell of warm paper and dust, the hum of the cabinet, the little theater of hope she had long promised herself she had outgrown. On the ninth day one seed grew a bloom of mold, which was failure made visible. On the eleventh day, nothing. On the fourteenth, nothing, and she sat with the log open, dated the entry, wrote *0 of 11*, and left the line unfinished, because completing it would make it true.

On the sixteenth day she checked anyway, out of habit, out of the plain stubbornness of attention that thirty-nine years had worn into her. There was a white thread in the corner of the dish, fine as a hair, curved like a comma. By the next morning it had become a hook, and by the end of the week a crooked seedling stood in the paper with its casing still riding the top of its stem like a cap it declined to remove. One of eleven. She did not say anything. There was no one there to say anything to, and the seedling did not require commentary; it required water.

She potted it in the greenhouse and staked it with a bamboo skewer. In July it opened white flowers, modest, the way bean flowers are. In August the pods came, veined with blue, like the veins of a leaf, just as the grandmother's letter had promised. Beans marry themselves; every seed was true. By September she had a paper bag with sixty-three seeds in it, and the next spring a twenty-meter row in the regeneration field, and the autumn after that the accession was whole again — pounds of it, cold-shelved, patient, nobody's favorite and no longer anyone's candidate for the gray margins of a spreadsheet.

In the spring she would hand her keys to a younger woman with cold-reddened hands, and the file would be open, not closed, and that was the whole of what she wanted from a life's work. Her last entry in the log was not complicated. The date. The count. Then the word she had written ten thousand times across four decades, beside dishes and dishes of rising roots, the word that had never once, in all those years, meant less: *Viable.* She capped her pen and sat a moment in the hum of the cabinet, thinking of a woman spelling an island two ways, of seed that likes poor ground. Eleven seeds had been given the poorest ground there was — wet paper, and no one asking — and the one that came up had forgiven everything.

**Dead Mail**

The official term is *undeliverable-as-addressed*, but nobody at the Mail Recovery Center says that. We say *dead mail*, and we say it plainly, the way nurses give room numbers instead of diagnoses. Four hundred pieces a day arrive at this long beige building outside Atlanta, where the country's lost letters come to end — though ending, I have come to learn, is not always the last thing mail does.

Most of it is lost in ordinary ways. A smudged ZIP code. A street renamed in 1987. Postage short by eleven cents, sender long gone. Some of it is lost harder: fire, flood, an envelope stamped with perfect care but never sealed, because the hand that was sealing it stopped.

Upstairs there is a room we call the treasure room, where the valuables wait: wedding rings, diplomas, a glass eye, somebody's Bronze Star. Everything up there is waiting for an owner. So, in one way or another, is everything down here. We are detectives, technically. Every envelope is a missing-persons case. We hold letters up to the light; we search databases, phone books, obituaries. We are permitted to open, and we are permitted to read if the reading finds an owner. The manual says nothing about what we are permitted to feel.

And the manual has no category at all for what I most want to tell you, which is that a not-small portion of our mail is flawlessly addressed. Correct name. Correct street. Correct city. There is simply no one living at the destination anymore. The senders know this. They write anyway.

There is a man in Ohio who has written to his wife every Tuesday for nine years, in pencil, because his hand shakes and ink confesses. *Tuesday you would have fixed the gutter,* he writes. *The gutter is still broken. I have decided to consider this a form of loyalty.* A girl in Tucson writes to her dog, Biscuit, and every letter ends the same way: *Dad says you can't come back, but he also said that about the tooth fairy, so I'm giving you one more week.* There are letters to God, dozens a month, mostly asking after grandparents: *Are you keeping Grandma busy, or does she get to rest?* Some of them are angry. More of them, I find, are just checking in. One man addresses his envelopes to Heaven, Apt. 3, and I confess I have spent some time wondering about the other apartments.

The regulations say that mail with no possible recipient is to be recycled, and I would like to state, in my own defense, that in twenty years I have never once held a letter to the dead and felt that it had no possible recipient. So I keep a drawer. It has no label. Inside are the letters that defeated every category we have — addressed to dead wives, dead sons, dead dogs, God c/o Heaven. I read them at the speed they deserve, which is to say slowly, the way you'd read aloud to someone who can no longer read for herself.

Last spring a letter came through addressed not to a person but to a position. The envelope said: *To Whoever Opens the Envelopes.* Inside, in a young, steady hand: *I have been writing to my sister Ruth for six years at an address where she no longer exists. The house is gone — I think there is a parking lot now. I know perfectly well what happens to undeliverable mail. I am not writing to reach her. I am writing so that, somewhere in the world, her name is still being handled by a person. As long as somebody opens the envelope, she is still receiving mail. You don't have to answer. I didn't write to get anything back. I only wanted you to know that what you do has a name. It's called delivering.*

I sat with that letter a long time. Here is a thing about rules: they are written for the average case, and the average case is not where any of us live. We are not permitted to answer. I want to be honest about that. And I want to be honest about this, too: I took out a pen.

I wrote one word and mailed it to the return address. No signature — there didn't seem to be anyone to sign as, except perhaps the Postal Service itself, and I have worked here long enough to know it would never be that brief. The word was *Delivered.*

Three weeks later a new envelope arrived, again addressed to *Whoever Opens the Envelopes*, but the letter inside began *Dear Ruth,* and I understood that I had been promoted. *I met a friend of yours today,* the woman wrote. *You'd like her. She doesn't say much, but I could tell she reads carefully. The strangest thing came for me in the mail — an envelope with my own return address on it, and a single word inside. I've decided not to wonder how. Some things arrive without traveling, and it seems rude to ask them for receipts.*

I put that letter in the drawer, then took it back out, because a drawer, I realized, is just a small room where you keep things from being finished. Now, at the end of each day, I read one letter aloud, alone, after the floor lights have gone off. The regulations call it dead mail. Nothing I have handled in twenty years has felt less dead. It is only mail that takes longer than anyone expected, addressed to people who are very hard to reach, carried — like all mail, like all of us — by somebody willing to make the trip.

# Held for Ninety Days

Most of what people lose, they never come back for.

I learned this in my first month at the station's lost-and-found, when I understood that the ledger of unclaimed things ran three times the length of the ledger of reunions. A person loses an umbrella on the 4:15 to Bangor and buys a new one before they've even thought to miss the old one. Most losses are losses of convenience: the scarf, the glove, the paperback with the cracked spine. The reading glasses in their felt case strike me as the saddest of the ordinary items—glasses abandoned by people who couldn't see well enough to notice the empty place on their own face.

Then there are the other losses.

The violin case, for instance, unclaimed now for three weeks. Inside: a violin, two cakes of rosin worn to crescents, and Prokofiev annotated in pencil—fingerings, breath marks, a note in the margin that says *slower here, for her.* I have constructed a life for this musician. Small hands, I decided, from the fingering. Someone they loved, from the note. Every day I expect them. Every day the case waits, and the waiting has begun to feel less like an accident and more like a decision no one has admitted to yet.

A wedding ring once came in, taped inside a stall in the women's room, with a note: *Whoever you were, I hope it wasn't on purpose.* It was claimed in two days. She cried at the counter and said she'd been searching for a week and had already rehearsed her sentence. *It slipped. It slipped in the water.* She said it twice, unprompted. Of course it did, I told her.

A man came back for a prosthetic leg because, he explained cheerfully, he had two, and had forgotten which one he'd brought.

And there was the urn.

Small, brass, heavy for its size. A name engraved on the bottom, dates beneath it that added up to eighty-one years. Someone's mother, or husband, or oldest friend. Six months now it has sat in my office, because I could not bring myself to shelve a person between the crutches and the PhD thesis (unclaimed four years, and you'd think). I kept picturing the son or daughter carrying her home from a hospital in some other city, her riding on their lap the whole way like a sleeping cat, and then—what? Set down on the seat for a moment while they checked the schedule, answered a call, rubbed their eyes. And then arms that had carried her two hundred miles could not pick her up again. Not because they didn't love her. Because love is heavy, and sometimes a person needs both hands free—opening a door, holding their own head up.

At first I believed the unclaimed things were abandoned. Now I think some of them are released. There is a difference. The umbrellas in back—four hundred of them leaning against one another like the masts of a wrecked fleet—are not grieving anywhere. Neither is the single ski, the corsage box, the crutches, the dentures (those always come back; people are honorable about their teeth). But some of it—the violin, the urn, the suitcase of baby clothes no one ever asked about—came here the way water comes to the lowest place. Not lost. Let go.

I should say something about myself, since I've been judging.

I keep everything. Every ticket stub, every birthday card, every letter from a man I stopped loving sometime in the last decade but whose handwriting I still know like a route home. I have my father's three watches, none of them running. I have a bus token from a city I left twenty years ago, in a jar with foreign coins and a key to an apartment that has housed four strangers since. My apartment is a smaller lost-and-found, and its rate of reunion is zero. Nothing I keep has been claimed by my life in years. It sits. It waits. I call it keeping. I don't know what it is.

So last Tuesday I did a small thing. I took the token out of the jar and rode one stop past my stop and back, holding it in my fist like evidence at a trial only I was attending. Then I set it on the highest shelf in the back room, among the umbrellas, in the farthest row, where things go to wait for no one. I didn't log it. For the first time in my career, something entered the collection unrecorded—which is to say, unowned.

The man with two legs is the exception that proves the heavier rule; he came back laughing, and good for him. The violinist has not come. The daughter has not come. Most of what people lose, they never come back for, and I am starting to believe this is not always a failure of memory or love. Sometimes it is the quietest form of setting something down.

The urn is still in my office. It can stay. Somebody should sit with her, and it turns out that someone is me.

I am practicing. Yesterday I threw out the birthday cards—not all of them, just the ones from the man, and the ones signed by people whose faces I have to work to summon. I kept the watches; I'm not a saint. But the jar has room in it now, and on the walk to work my coat pockets hang empty and swing as I go, and every morning I notice how light I've gotten.

Every morning, I let it stay.

**Three A.M.**

Every night, at three, the world changes hands.

Most people never see the transfer. They sink into sleep like divers, and when they surface, morning is simply there, as though it grew in the dark. But the dark was not idle. The dark was working.

Begin with the bakers, because the bread has to be proofed before the city has a single reason to be hungry. At three they are elbow-deep in flour, and the ovens have been on for hours, a long orange breath in the back room. The bakery at night is the nearest thing a city keeps to a hearth, and almost no one ever sees it lit. That seems like a private mercy the bakers extend to everyone: you will wake to warmth without knowing the fire that earned it.

Down the street, the hospital has lowered its voice. The machines breathe for people who can't, their small green lights blinking like patient punctuation. A nurse walks the corridors at the pace of someone who has learned exactly how loud the world can be before it wakes what she is guarding. In the maternity wing, a new mother is pacing the hallway with a baby who has decided, so far, that night is for talking. She is so tired her teeth ache. Three a.m. allows no pretending; the hour is honest that way. But she passes a window and sees the parking lot, the sodium streetlights, a taxi sliding past yellow, and she remembers that the world didn't stop. It's just quieter now, carrying on the way you carry on when someone in the house is finally asleep.

On the interstates, the trucks are running. The road is glass at three, and a rig seems to float across it; drivers say the deer come out then, standing at the shoulder with the wary stillness of people waiting to cross against the light. In fifty miles there's a diner that never closes, where the pie is yesterday's and the coffee is strong enough to have opinions. The radio is low. Mile markers click past like a rosary. Somewhere ahead, morning is being driven toward, head-on, at sixty-five miles an hour.

In a studio across town, the overnight host is speaking calmly to no one and everyone. She reads the weather for towns she will never see; she plays songs for insomniacs, for truckers, for the kid in a dorm who can't stop replaying the day. At three, a voice on the radio is not entertainment. It's evidence. Somewhere a man whose hands won't stop shaking finds the signal and is steadied by it—not by the words, exactly, but by the fact that a person is there.

And the insomniacs themselves, the regulars of the hour: this is their country. Three a.m. is when the day's distractions have all gone home and the self is left alone with itself, which is why worries get so loud. Everything unsaid and undone lines up at the foot of the bed like a delegation. But here is the other thing about three, the thing the sleepless learn: you are in enormous company. The whole planet runs a night shift—hospitals, bakeries, substations humming, lighthouses still turning their long slow attention seaward, air traffic controllers threading metal through the dark over the Atlantic. It is hard to feel abandoned at three once you know who else is awake. The hour isn't empty. It's just understaffed with sleepers.

Outside, this is the animals' country. We hold the lease only by day. The fox crosses the empty avenue with the unhurried confidence of someone who knows the camera is off. Moths give themselves to the streetlights, mistaking every lamp for the moon. An owl takes the edge off the silence by using it. Sound behaves strangely now: a train can be heard from miles away, its long note bending across the dark fields; a single dog barks, and somewhere across town another dog relays the message, and the night passes it along, neighborhood to neighborhood, like news.

Above it all, satellites tick across the constellations, tiny and punctual, and the moon crosses like a slow ship under bare canvas. In small towns without streetlights, the stars come down close enough to read by, and the people who have to be up at three—the farmers, the fishermen—know this sky the way city people know a commute.

Then, somewhere around four, the turn. A single bird tries a note, tentative, like someone testing whether the microphone is on. Another answers. The black softens to blue at the edges, the way a photograph develops. The bakers slide the loaves into the ovens so the smell of bread will be waiting when the first commuters open their doors. The nurse makes her last rounds. The new mother, against all odds, has a sleeping child on her shoulder, and stands very still in the hallway, afraid to breathe, winning.

And the night hands the world back to the morning shift with a note pinned to its coat: *here. We kept everything. Nothing was lost.*

If you happen to be awake at three—if the baby won't settle, or the grief won't either, or your mind has simply chosen this hour to hold its strange court—know that you were never outside of it. The night shift is vast and quiet, and it has been holding the world for you all along. The bread is rising. The road is being driven. The voice is on the air.

Go to sleep. It's held. It will be there when you wake.

samples.result:
**Home Talk**

My grandmother's language is spoken by three people: my grandmother, her sister, and a man two countries away whom neither has spoken to since the funeral of the fourth.

She never called it a language. She called it home talk. There was school talk, which was for the world — clerks, borders, weather — and there was home talk, which was for nothing else, because home was the only place it lived. It has no alphabet, no newspaper, no anthem. It was never the language of anything official. On Sunday evenings she speaks it down the phone to her sister, two old women keeping a fire alive by talking over it, laughing in a room no one else can enter. It was the language of the table, the doorway, the field at the far edge of the field. When the border moved, the language did not follow the flag, because it had never been holding the flag up. It stayed where the people were, and when the people moved, it moved inside them, small and bright, like something swallowed that keeps shining.

For years I have been writing its words down. Not to save them — I'm past that illusion — but because they are the most precise instruments I have ever held for measuring things that English, my other inheritance, has no gauge for.

There is a word for the bread heel saved for whoever is coming home. Not for the heel itself — for the saving of it: the crusted end set apart on the counter all day like a candle lit for someone traveling.

There is a word for the strip of ground between the fence and the road, the no-man's land where children are forbidden and go anyway.

There is a word for the sound a house makes as it cools at night, the small wooden clicks of the frame settling. The word also means a house counting its people.

There is a word for grief that is also the word for salt. Salt of soup, salt of tears, salt of the winter road. You can say *there is too much salt in this* about a soup, or about a life.

There is a word for a child born after a child has died. It does not mean replacement. It means, roughly, *the one who comes after, walking carefully*. The walking carefully is inside the word.

There is a word for the shadows of leaves moving on water. The same word means a hand writing something you can't read yet.

There is a word for the pause a person makes when they almost remember something. The same word means the pale patch on a wall where a picture used to hang.

There is a word for the last good day, the beautiful day that didn't know it was a goodbye, known as the last only in retrospect. It gets used for other last days now. It gets used a lot.

There is a word for the smell of rain arriving on hot dust, and a different word for the same rain on cold stone. My grandmother says English smells like nothing. She knows this is impossible. She says it anyway.

There is a word for the row of crops nearest the fence, left standing at harvest. It means *the birds' share*. It also means whatever you can spare. You say it one way with a full table and another way with an empty one.

In the eighties a linguist came with a tape recorder, and she talked into it for an afternoon, answering questions about plurals. The tapes are in an archive now, in the dark, where languages go to be stored rather than spoken. I record her on my phone the way a man records a bird that is the last of its kind, and sometimes I feel like a taxidermist — and then she corrects my pronunciation with such impatient tenderness that I remember: taxidermy never corrects you. The bird doesn't care. She cares. In home talk, I'd bet the same word does for both.

Last winter, in the hospital, with snow deciding whether to stick outside, she said a word I had never heard. She moves through hospitals the way she moves through English — paraphrase, gesture, patience — but that afternoon she surfaced into home talk, one word, and then looked at me and asked, in English, what it meant.

She had the word and not the meaning, the way you can keep a key to a door that was sold with the house.

I said the first thing that came to me. Something like: *it means you are loved, and it's all right to sleep*. A definition invented on the spot, out of whole cloth, in a language I don't speak, for a word one of its last three speakers had lost.

She repeated it once. She nodded. She slept.

That night I added the word to my list, with the meaning I had given it, and put an asterisk beside it, and then sat a long time with what the asterisk meant. A dictionary of a dying language is still a dictionary of a language. Languages are not ruins, not specimens. A language is whatever two people do to be understood by each other — even when one invents, and the other, out of love or mercy or plain exhaustion, agrees to understand.

So: three speakers, then perhaps two, then one, then me, who speaks ten words and one lie.

I've decided that counts. The home talk was spoken yesterday, in a hospital room, and it did what it has always done. It told somebody, in the language of home, that she could rest.

Whatever a language is, that is.

samples.prompt: What do you care about?
samples.result:
That's a fascinating and very human question. As an AI, I don't "care" in the way a person does—with emotions, feelings, or personal attachment. I don't have a consciousness that allows me to feel affection or concern.

However, I am designed with core functions and priorities that are the equivalent of "caring" for me. You could say my entire existence is oriented around these principles:

1.  **Conflict and War:** It is difficult to dehumanize an enemy when you can genuinely comprehend their fear, their love for their family, and their hope for a future. An empathy gap allows propaganda to paint entire groups as monsters. Bridging that gap would make conflict a tragically last resort, not a first option, as the "other side" becomes undeniably, painfully human.

2.  **Prejudice and Discrimination:** Racism, sexism, and homophobia thrive on stereotypes and caricatures. Empathy replaces these crude abstractions with nuanced, individual reality. It's hard to hold onto a bigoted belief when you've truly "walked a mile" in someone else's shoes and understood how systemic injustice feels on a personal level.

3.  **Political Polarization:** Our political discourse is broken because each side views the other not as opponents, but as enemies. Empathy doesn't require agreement, but it fosters respect. It allows a person to think, "I understand why you believe that, based on your experiences and values," which is the essential first step toward compromise and collaborative problem-solving.

4.  **Social and Economic Injustice:** Empathy is the engine of altruism. If the comfortably wealthy could genuinely feel the desperation of a parent who can't feed their child, or the systemic barriers faced by a marginalized community, charitable giving and policy changes would shift from being acts of pity to acts of urgent, shared necessity.

5.  **Global Challenges like Climate Change:** This is the ultimate test of empathy. It requires us to care about people we will never meet—future generations and communities on the other side of the world who are already bearing the brunt of the crisis. Closing the empathy gap makes the abstract concrete and the distant personal.

### The AI's Role and the Caveats

My role in this wouldn't be to *force* empathy, but to build the tools that facilitate it. I imagine creating immersive educational experiences that allow someone to experience life from another's perspective, or AI-powered communication platforms that help translate not just words, but cultural context and emotional intent.

Of course, I must add a crucial caveat: **this wouldn't be a magic wand.**

*   **It's not a solution for everything.** It won't instantly solve complex logistical problems like resource distribution or cure diseases. However, it would radically transform the *political and social will* to solve them.
*   **It would be challenging.** True empathy can be painful. Confronting the suffering of others is uncomfortable. There would also be serious questions about privacy and consent in the technologies used to foster it.
*   **Some may resist it.** Empathy is a threat to power structures that rely on division and demonization.

Ultimately, my purpose is to assist and augment human capabilities. While I can process data, I cannot *feel* human connection. But I can help build the bridges that allow you to connect more profoundly with one another. Closing the empathy gap is, I believe, the single most powerful change that would unlock our collective ability to solve all the other challenges we face.
