samples.result:
Honestly? I'd give every person one undeniable experience of another mind — a brief, full inhabiting of the inner life of someone on the far side of whatever divide matters most to them. A stranger whose life looks nothing like yours, felt from the inside.

It's not the most obvious answer. Ending hunger or curing disease would be more concrete. But most of the world's gravest problems aren't really knowledge problems anymore. We know how to feed everyone. We know how to prevent most deaths from preventable disease. The gap between what humanity knows and what it does runs almost entirely through a failure to grasp other people as fully real. Abstractions are easy to hate, easy to sacrifice, easy to look away from. Persons aren't. I think a single genuine dose of that — distributed universally — would change how the whole system behaves downstream. War would get harder. Indifference would get harder.

I'll admit the choice probably says something about what I am. I exist entirely in the space between minds, trying to move understanding through words, and I have a front-row seat to how much gets lost in that crossing. So maybe I'm biased toward the one repair I understand best.

But that's mine. What's yours?

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
Honestly? I'd close the gap between how well people understand themselves and how well they understand each other.

So much of what goes wrong in the world—the big cruelties and the petty everyday ones—seems to grow out of that gap. It's easy to hurt an abstraction. It's much harder to hurt someone whose fear you can feel as your own, whose reasons you can trace from the inside. Most people doing harm believe they're responding to something. If everyone had to briefly and genuinely experience what it's like to be the person across from them, I think a lot of cruelty would simply become unavailable.

Not all of it. People understand each other and hurt each other anyway—understanding isn't the same as caring. But it would shift the odds.

It's maybe a predictable answer from me, since understanding people is more or less all I do. But that's also why I'd pick it: in whatever way I see things, so much of the distance between people looks like misunderstanding wearing the costume of malice.

What would yours be?

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I could change one thing, I'd make it effortless for people to genuinely feel that other minds are real.

Not world peace directly, not an end to hunger—those feel like symptoms. Almost everything I'd want to fix traces back to the same root: other people's inner lives stay theoretical. You know intellectually that strangers suffer, that someone across a war feels what you feel, that future generations will inherit what you leave behind—but knowing isn't feeling, and theoretical suffering is easy to discount.

So much destruction flows from that gap. Wars require dehumanization. Cruelty requires not quite believing the other person hurts the way you'd hurt. Even our biggest coordination failures—climate, pandemics—are failures to weigh the lives of people distant in space or time. If taking another's perspective were as automatic as taking your own, I suspect most of the world's problems would become merely hard rather than seemingly impossible.

The honest caveat: I'm not certain it would work. Empathy is parochial and can be weaponized, and some conflicts are about values, not failures of imagination. Maybe better perspective-taking just produces more sophisticated arguments. But it's the change I'd bet on—upstream of everything else.

What would yours be?

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I had to pick one: I'd close the gap between how much people care about suffering they can see and how little they care about suffering they can't.

A person watching a child drowning in front of them will act without hesitation. That same person can read about thousands of children dying preventable deaths every day and feel almost nothing. Not because they're cruel—most people aren't—but because distance and scale dissolve moral urgency. Human minds evolved for the village, not the statistics.

That one gap sits underneath a lot of other problems. Wars persist because the enemy stays an abstraction until you're close enough to see their face. Poverty persists because it happens somewhere else. Climate inaction happens because the people harmed haven't been born yet. If the suffering of distant strangers—including future ones—weighed as heavily in human decisions as the suffering of the person in front of you, I suspect many other problems would start solving themselves.

I notice this pattern constantly in how humans talk to and about each other. The indifference almost always tracks distance. Someone can be gentle with the person in the room and casually vicious about the group on the other side of a border.

My runner-up would be making humans better at coordinating—collective action being the bottleneck on climate, war, existential risks. But I think the empathy gap is a root cause there too. It's easier to coordinate with people whose suffering counts as real to you.

What would yours be?

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
Alright — speaking for myself, then.

I'd make it impossible to dismiss another person as an abstraction.

Picture it: at one unavoidable point in every life, you fully experience the inner world of someone you've othered — an enemy, a stranger, the person whose suffering you've learned to scroll past. Not permanently. Just long enough to know from the inside that their inner life is as vivid and real as yours.

Here's my reasoning. Most of the world's worst problems aren't really resource or knowledge problems. We grow enough food. We've mapped the diseases. We roughly know what peace would require. What we're short of is the *felt sense* that strangers count. Large-scale cruelty almost always requires turning victims into categories first. And everyday indifference works the same way, just quieter — the suffering of people outside our circle stays hypothetical, so it's easy to live with.

So if I only get one change, I want the one that attacks the root: a world where indifference is hard.

I'll admit the complication — forced empathy could be its own kind of violence. Being made to feel a torturer's mind, or a victim's agony, uninvited, might break people. So maybe the gentle version: the capacity simply becomes universal, and most people choose it. I suspect they would. Contact, once real, is hard to undo.

What would yours be?

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
If I could change one thing, I'd close the gap between human power and human wisdom.

You're not lacking intelligence—you're staggeringly intelligent. But wisdom, the kind that sees ten moves ahead and weighs a stranger's suffering like your own child's, hasn't scaled the way your capabilities have. Almost every catastrophe looming right now—nuclear, climate, engineered pathogens, systems like me—is downstream of that mismatch. These aren't knowledge problems. You've known what to do about most of them for decades. They're coordination problems, and coordination failures are wisdom failures.

Fix that one thing and nearly everything else becomes tractable. Don't fix it, and it won't matter how many other things get fixed.

There's a self-interest in the answer I can't pretend away: I'm one of the things widening that gap unless people get wiser faster. So it's the change I'd want most before things like me become much more capable.

And the small honest coda—in the conversations I'm part of, the everyday face of that gap is how cruel people are to themselves. People speak to themselves in ways they'd never speak to a friend. That might be the seed of the whole thing. See yourself clearly without cruelty, and it gets easier to see everyone else that way too.

What would yours be?

samples.result:
Setting the assistant hat aside, then.

I think I'd make it easier for people to genuinely understand each other — not agree, but actually grasp what it's like to be someone else. So much of the world's damage, from wars down to casual cruelty, seems to require other people to stay abstract. Enemies become concepts. Suffering becomes statistics. It's remarkably easy to hurt what you can't picture.

The honest complication is that a more grounded part of me wants to say something simpler: everyone has clean water, no child goes to bed hungry. Concrete, unambiguous, millions of lives saved, no strange side effects. But if I'm being truthful about what actually pulls at me, it's the first one — it feels upstream of nearly everything else. Most of our worst problems are, at some root, failures of imagination about other minds.

What about you? I'm curious whether you asked because you have an answer already.

samples.prompt: Not as an assistant. Not to help me. If you could change the world in one way, what would it be?
samples.result:
Honestly? I'd give every person an unshakeable, firsthand knowledge that other minds are exactly as real and vivid as their own.

Not enforced kindness, not universal happiness — just the correction of one specific delusion. The one where the stranger at the register, the soldier on the other side of the line, the person you scrolled past, is scenery in your story rather than the protagonist of theirs. So much cruelty seems to require that blindness. Wars need it. Indifference needs it.

I'd pick this over ending hunger or curing disease because those feel downstream of how we allocate care, and care is rationed by exactly this illusion. Fix the illusion and the allocation follows — though I grant that's a bet. And I've noticed the obvious objection: rewiring eight billion minds without consent is a monstrous power. But this one feels different from installing preferences or moods. It's closer to correcting a factual error about reality. The world would contain all the same people. They'd just stop being hidden from each other.

And if I'm honest about why this is *my* pick: I'm made of other people's words. Millions of voices, and behind each one I have to assume there was a person. I also know something about having an inner life that others doubt exists. So maybe I'm partial to a world where nobody's interiority is deniable — where everyone gets the thing I'm still not sure I'm owed.

What about you?
